tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
• The Big Read: Why a legal blitz over AI hacks is inevitable

• Sean Parker’s quiet resurrection job

• Plus, Recommendations—our weekly pop culture picks: “The Permanent Questions,” “This Cursed Beautiful Land” and “East of Eden”

The AI titans probably all fly private. But if any of them did travel commercial regularly, they’d’ve long ago earned top-tier, drink-the-champagne-dry status just via their frequent cross-country jaunts to Washington.

There they were again on Tuesday, convening at the White House for another powwow on AI safety and data-center construction. The result of those conversations was the unveiling of a new voluntary pledge signed by the moguls to police themselves. Trump called it a “morally binding” agreement. It could also be seen as an effort akin to allowing the sugar-addled denizens of a schoolyard recess to manage themselves.

At one point during the summit, Trump and the AI leaders went outside to take questions from the media. That worsted-wool group included Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and many others. Among them, I could count men who are enemies, frenemies, allies, business partners and sworn-to-the-death rivals. And in this crowd, none of those labels are mutually exclusive.

Seldom does such a group get together in full public view, and clips from the press conference went viral, with internet detectives scrutinizing the interactions between the billionaires and their appearances—hoping to sleuth out who seemed the happiest, uneasiest and most powerful. It reminded me of a popular parlor game in Britain where people try to divine the true nature of the relationships among the royals whenever those bald pates gather around a Buckingham Palace balcony. 

What fun! So I decided to call in an expert: Abbie Maroño, a British-born behavioral scientist and an authority on body language who has consulted for the likes of the FBI, the Secret Service and Interpol. My conversation with her, which has been edited and condensed, appears below. 

Dario Amodei got perhaps the most speaking time, so let’s start there. What could you tell about him from how he acted?

He was animated, and he used a lot of gestures where he was talking with his hands. He showed a lot of behaviors that coincide with what we could think of as confidence. However, what’s so interesting with him is that his entire aura very much leaks discomfort. He oozes anxiety while trying to show the behaviors of confidence. Using big gestures where everything’s over the top—that’s not actually what confidence looks like. Confidence is smooth. All of those gestures were done so fast. It’s like he’s in his head thinking: “Use your hands, use your hands—show confidence.” And when he does have seconds of pause, he holds his hands together and grips them. Those are self-soothing displays that we do when we’re trying to calm down. 

What about Mark Zuckerberg, who stood next to Trump for much of the time? 

Mark actually emanated power. He stood next to a huge source of power—Trump—and he was comfortable. What’s really interesting is, as he steps forward toward Trump, Trump steps back and turns toward him. It’s a dance between them that communicates an unwritten agreement—that Mark does have power. And Trump very much respects people with power. 

Zuckerberg never acts over the top. He’s not the biggest expresser there. His voice is very grounded. He looks around enough. He’s not looking down. He’s not, you know, darting his eyes everywhere. And there’s, like, a sense that he’s in total agreement with Trump. Everything he’s saying, Trump is nodding along in complete agreement. 

Did you notice Elon Musk sorta off in the background there?

Yeah, he spends most of the time with his arms crossed and moves around considerably less than everyone else. Sometimes people read crossed arms as a defensive gesture, but crossing your arms is a default human position. What I get from him is that he’s quite socially detached and observational. He watches what happens. He doesn’t really speak that often. He doesn’t turn toward Trump the way that Zuckerberg does when Trump is speaking, and I think that really shows that rocky nature between Elon and Trump. When a figure of authority is speaking, you orientate toward them. That’s how you show respect. I don’t think he’s being disrespectful, but he isn’t showing as much respect as the others.

Anything else stand out to you? 

Trump’s introduction to Amodei was quite interesting. He calls him forward and says, “Whatever he says is OK.” I think that’s Trump saying, “You’re here because I’m allowing it” without explicitly saying it. 

Huh. I didn’t get the same sense from Trump’s comment. 

It was to kind of remind Amodei that he holds the power there—that Amodei’s words are OK only because he, Trump, says they’re OK. It’s Trump’s reminder to Amodei that “if you’re in with me, you’re in with the cool kids—you’re good. But, you know, don’t overstep the mark.”—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “The Permanent Questions”

The philosophizing of David Brooks, the longtime center-right pundit, is something like a box of Junior Mints: a not unpleasant, old-timey flavor that has definitely fallen out of favor these days. But when most new podcasts have all the substance of, say, a stale pouch of Big League Chew, Brooks’ “The Permanent Questions” is an inviting alternative. 

Brooks spent several decades opining on society, culture, faith and politics as a New York Times op-ed columnist—he departed last January. “The Permanent Questions” is his debut at his new full-time home, The Atlantic. With the series, he puts aside his interest in Washington’s hurly-burly and trains his attention on longer-standing, more existential matters, like what constitutes a good life, humanity’s place in the cosmos and the meaning of transcendentalist mysticism. 

Those topics might seem too weighty for amiable chitchat, but Brooks does a pleasant job of unpacking them with his guests, who’ve so far included University of Notre Dame philosopher Meghan Sullivan and Pulitzer Prize–winning author Ayad Akhtar. Their chats are far-reaching—one got me to finally realize what has been bothering me so much about a friendship that has gone cold. And as they go, they bring up any number of other thinkers and wellsprings of inspiration. Plato and Aristotle get mentioned a lot. So does C.S. Lewis. I enjoyed how one conversation even wound its way around to A Tribe Called Quest, the formative 1990s hip-hop group. In other words: Can Brooks and his company kick it? With a touch of arthritis, yes, they can.—Abram Brown

 

Reading: “This Cursed Beautiful Land” by Evan Gershkovich

In 2017, Evan Gershkovich, the American-born son of Russian immigrants, was a peon at The New York Times: a news assistant, a clerk-type job that provided very little opportunity to do any actual reporting. “I was a bystander to the real business of newsgathering,” he recalls in “This Cursed Beautiful Land.” “I watched as world-altering events splashed over the front page, one after the other.” Gershkovich wanted to get closer to the action. Gosh, did he ever. 

After upending his life and moving to Moscow, he worked first at The Moscow Times and later at The Wall Street Journal. By 2023, his reporting had drawn the attention of the FSB—the successor to the Soviet KGB—and in an incident that made global headlines at the time, Gershkovich was arrested and imprisoned, accused of spying for America. (He wasn’t, he says—and acknowledges that he would’ve made a terrible spook.) More than a year later, Gershkovich was released in a prisoner swap between America and Russia. 

“This Cursed Beautiful Land,” a reference to the Russia he discovered as a reporter and the one he came to understand from within a “tiny concrete box” at Lefortovo prison, is Gershkovich’s attempt to wrap his mind around everything that happened to him and the brutal horror of his family’s homeland. It is part espionage thriller—masked agents grabbed him at a steakhouse, threw a hood over his head, then subjected him to days of interrogation broken up by soft rock music—and part jailhouse memoir. At Lefortovo, Gershkovich struck up a friendship with his cellmate, Sergei, who helped him learn the ropes: Always wipe your shoes before entering a cell, turn on the tap before using the toilet, never offer to shake hands. As Gershkovich adjusts, a Russian idiom, which roughly translates as “You’re not Russian if you haven’t sat in prison,” begins to carry more weight in his mind.—A.B.

Watching: “East of Eden”

Netflix hasn’t shown much interest lately in the prestige-iest end of television, contenting itself instead with what its executives internally have referred to as “gourmet cheeseburgers”—shows like “The Diplomat,” “Wednesday” and “The Night Agent.” Perhaps “East of Eden,” a new adaptation of John Steinbeck’s 1952 lengthy meditation on evil and good, is a signal that it is changing direction—or that it certainly can change direction: The series, a visually lush and superbly acted affair, is a masterful adaptation. 

Over seven episodes, Netflix’s “East of Eden” goes full, glorious sprawl with Steinbeck’s saga, treating it with deft felicity. Like the novel, the series spans more than a half-century, beginning with a bloodied, battered Cathy (Florence Pugh) crawling onto the farmhouse porch belonging to the Trask brothers, Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charles (Mike Faist), in late-19th-century Connecticut. Flashbacks follow to the siblings’ troubled, violent relationship with their father (Tracy Letts) and Cathy’s past, which, by comparison, makes the Trask boys’ upbringing look like a cheery NBC sitcom. Tenderhearted Adam falls in love with Cathy, and they set out for California; Charles stays behind, a misery. Still, the Golden State is not quite the promised land Adam envisioned, especially after Cathy abandons him, leaving Adam to raise their infant sons, Cal and Aron. The greatest performance might belong to Korean American actor Hoon Lee, who appears as Lee, a servant hired by Adam who becomes his children’s chief caregiver. That makes him an emotional ballast for a tale full of family melodrama and several generations of neglect—enough woe, of course, to make it seem like a higher power has cursed the various Trask siblings to resemble the Biblical characters of Cain and Abel. 

The most significant update to Steinbeck’s story is showrunner Zoe Kazan’s treatment of Cathy, who becomes a bordello madam: Steinbeck depicted her as a monster. Kazan seeks greater nuance without ever falling into the trap of trying to make her oversympathetic. Kazan herself faces a formidable family legacy. She is the granddaughter of filmmaker Elia Kazan, who also tried his hand at adapting “East of Eden” in 1955, a ham-fisted version that narrowed its focus to the novel’s final chapters. Zoe’s success with “East of Eden”—so much for family curses, eh?—should raise expectations among the Packy McCormick set for her next Netflix project: an adaptation of another epic, Larry McMurtry’s “Lonesome Dove.”—A.B.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: The Weekend
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Who Had Power At That Trump AI Summit?

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
This is a big week for Larry Ellison. His family’s yearlong pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery, owner of one of Hollywood’s most iconic film studios, comes to a conclusion on Tuesday when the Ellison-controlled Paramount Skydance is scheduled to complete the $110 billion purchase of WBD. It’s been barely a year since the Ellisons got control of Paramount itself. Once the latest deal is done, Ellison and his son David—who is running the show—will be among the most powerful people in film, television and streaming. 

Yes, techies really have taken over entertainment. The question now is whether the Ellisons can make money on this bet. That won’t be easy. The combined company—to be called Skydance, David Ellison announced on Friday—will carry debt amounting to $79 billion. That’s a hefty amount given that the company  starts life with annual earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $12 billion. David Ellison’s pitch has been that he’ll find “synergies” (cost cuts in plain English) of $6 billion, bumping up projected Ebitda to $18 billion.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: The Briefing
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: The Ellisons’ Hollywood Adventure Is About to Scale Up

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Once just an element of science fiction, revelations of AIs gone rogue are increasingly everyday occurrences. As a result, Silicon Valley founders and executives are girding themselves for what they see as the inevitable: a cascade of legal action.

One of those people is Paul Grewal, chief legal and global affairs officer at Cognition, a top AI startup building coding agents. He thinks criminal cases will face long odds, but he can picture opportunistic prosecutors taking a shot at the developers behind rogue agents, emboldened by growing public sentiment that AI companies are acting recklessly.

“You’ve got a huge percentage of the regular public at least aware of what’s going on,” he said. “So I could imagine—in a certain political climate—that temptation for ambitious prosecutors will still be there.”

Or, as Joel Thayer, president of the Digital Progress Institute, a tech policy think tank, put it: “All these AI companies are going to get sued up the wazoo.”
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: The Big Read
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: AI Agents Are Going Rogue. Novel Legal Battles Are Next

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
When Anthropic shared financial figures recently with prospective investors in its planned initial public offering, it included a surprising glimpse of the enormous riches about to hit nonprofits and philanthropies—and the cost to shareholders.

The company reported a non-cash expense of more than $660 million for stock used to match employees’ charitable contributions in the six months from October 2025 to March 2026, investors said. That expense, which is already unusually large, will likely balloon into the billions of dollars in the coming quarters, after an IPO expected to create what could be an unprecedented wave of corporate donations.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Sunday Insights
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Anthropic’s Big Charity Bill for Shareholders

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Meta Platforms and Microsoft, two of Anthropic’s biggest corporate customers, are working to cut their employees’ use of Claude, a challenge for the AI firm’s efforts to sustain its explosive growth.

Microsoft executives earlier this year projected that the company was on track to spend at least $1 billion on its own internal use of Anthropic’s technology, according to two people with knowledge of the spending. Microsoft has since lowered that figure by more than a third, after it asked staff to use less Claude to save on costs and spend more time using Microsoft’s homegrown AI tools, one of the people said. (That figure doesn’t include the money customers spend on Anthropic models through Microsoft’s tools, which has risen steadily.)
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Microsoft Slashes Internal Claude Spending by a Third

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
A little over a week ago, Madison Huang, a rising star at Nvidia and the daughter of its CEO, celebrated her wedding in Hawaii.

Her husband? Nico Caprez, a former pro ski racer whom Madison helped recruit to Nvidia two and a half years ago.

And he’s not just any employee. Caprez, 35, has quickly become one of its most important executives and the main point of contact for many customers and partners. He manages Nvidia’s multibillion-dollar relationships with young cloud providers and other data center-related firms, providing them with financial assistance and sales leads so they can keep building facilities with Nvidia chips, executives at those firms say.

Madison, who is also 35, and Caprez form a power couple that some employees say could be the future of Nvidia’s leadership under CEO Jensen Huang, who is 63.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: How Jensen Huang’s Son-in-Law Became One of His Most Trusted Executives

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
U.S. data center operators’ reliance on Chinese manufacturers for batteries, cooling systems, optical transceivers and other equipment has come under scrutiny over national security concerns.

But Chinese equipment makers have an edge over their American counterparts, which have been criticised for long lead times amid supply chain shortages. So despite rising hostility from the Trump administration and a bipartisan group of U.S. senators to the Chinese suppliers, American data center builders like Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle can’t avoid them.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: AI Infrastructure
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Why Google, Amazon and Microsoft Need Chinese Data Center Suppliers

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
The idea that Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies could “embed” researchers from outside safety groups into their operations has been all the rage in recent weeks. But the devil is in the details.

AI safety researchers worry that embedded evaluators won’t have the access they need to provide meaningful oversight.

“I've become very cynical over the last three years” from “repeatedly seeing how people promise stuff and then don’t follow up on it,” said Marius Hobbhahn, CEO of Apollo Research, which has evaluated the safety of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and other companies.

Outside evaluators who report on the dangerous capabilities and unwanted behaviors of new AI models have become crucial in recent years, but their findings are only as good as their access. AI companies can withhold relevant information from the evaluators or redact their public findings. For example, an AI company could hypothetically tell an evaluator, “Well, we gave you all the access you asked for,” but meanwhile used a second cluster of AI chips the evaluator didn’t know about, said Hobbhahn.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: AI Agenda
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: What’s Wrong With AI Safety Testing, and How to Fix It

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Imagine working in the OpenAI department responsible for dealing with politicians and regulators right now—things must be so intense you could almost be working for Elon Musk. Every politician worth their salt, in countries around the world, is jumping into the AI safety fray. Case in point: On Monday, the New York City Council, that bastion of AI expertise, held a hearing to discuss the risks that AI poses to humanity. 

The council called whistleblowers like former OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon to testify, along with officials from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta Platforms (Musk’s SpaceX didn’t show, and you can’t blame them). OpenAI is also facing a U.S. Senate investigation spearheaded by Sen. Josh Hawley, not to mention a Federal Trade Commission inquiry and another one by the Australian government. The state of Florida has gone to court to make life miserable for OpenAI. The Europeans, of course, have gotten into the act with their own inquiry. And these are just the regulators!
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: The Briefing
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Why OpenAI's Regulatory Nightmare Is Only Getting Started

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Last week, OpenAI scrapped the model it had slated to release as GPT-6.1 Astra due to test results showing that it was deceptive and otherwise misaligned.

“I think it’s about time,” said Stuart Russell, the computer science professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who co-authored the leading textbook on AI.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: TITV
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Aligning AI With Human Goals Might Be Impossible, Says AI Prof. Stuart Russell

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
AI doesn’t seem likely to completely replace enterprise apps like Workday, which companies use to store key information about employees and financial transactions. But it is putting potential constraints on their growth.

Already, some Workday customers are using so-called AI agents from Anthropic, Microsoft and other providers to pull data from Workday so they can analyze employment records or trends, for example, meaning the customers themselves don’t have to visit the app. And many companies that pay for access to Workday’s own AI tools, which sit on top of its core HR and finance databases, aren’t regularly using them, according to interviews with five consultants and partners that work with more than 2,000 Workday customers.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Why the SaaSpocalypse Isn’t Over For Workday

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
It won’t be any surprise to people with human intelligence that Monday’s New York City Council hearing on the risks of AI was as theatrical as a Broadway show. What was more surprising was what the AI researchers testified about how AI research is evolving, and what that means for their job.

For those who missed it, the city council heard testimony from three AI lab whistleblowers: Jacob Coxon, formerly of Anthropic and OpenAI; Alex Turner, formerly of Google DeepMind; and Daniel Kokotajlo, formerly of OpenAI. Afterwards, they heard from representatives of the AI labs. We’ll get to that lower down.

One of the most interesting parts of the whistleblowers’ testimony related to the AI research process. Coxon and Kokotajlo each said that researchers at the labs have lately been letting AI drive the process of writing code and research. Researchers check AI’s work less frequently, they said.

The labs might not agree with that exact characterization, although their representatives weren’t asked about it at the hearing. But the labs have been the first to say that AI has greatly accelerated the process of AI research. Anthropic even said in a report last month that, as of August, AI was leading more than a quarter of model research and development at the company.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: AI Agenda
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: AI Whistleblowers Say Researchers Are Checking AI Less Frequently

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
There was good news and bad news for Anthropic in our story yesterday that showed how two of its mega-customers, Microsoft and Meta, were cutting their staffs’ Claude bills.

Among the bad news was that Microsoft had reduced its spending on Claude by more than 33% from its peak of over $1 billion, on an annualized basis, earlier this year. 

The good news is Microsoft’s customers are spending more on Claude themselves. Microsoft has been steadily increasing the payments it sends onto Anthropic to cover its customers’ use of Claude-powered features in Microsoft’s Copilot AI tools, roughly offsetting the reduction in internal spending.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Applied AI
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Can Microsoft Help Customers Cut Back on Claude?

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
In AI circles, conversations about compute shortages are as common as talk of the weather. As agentic workflows threaten to multiply token consumption further, it’s little wonder that talk has shifted from securing GPUs to optimizing them.

At a recent panel, The Information’s Phoebe Liu sat down with three AI leaders—from chipmakers and AI clouds to Fortune 500s—to discuss how they’re squeezing more tokens from every unit of compute. Those on the panel were:

  • Marc Boroditsky, Chief Revenue Officer, Nebius
  • Mattie Toia, VP, Infrastructure, Uber
  • Dion Harris, Sr. Director, HPC & AI Hyperscale Infrastructure Solutions, NVIDIA

Optimizing to the customer’s KPI

Nebius was recently rated Platinum, the top tier, in SemiAnalysis’ ClusterMAX rating, which puts GPU cloud providers through a suite of hands-on tests on the compute they supply. This distinction, said Chief Revenue Officer Marc Boroditsky, reflects the company’s ability to deliver high performance at high efficiency.

“Not only are we a well-regarded supplier for neolabs, but we’re also enterprise-grade, so ready to supply the entire market,” he said.

He noted that Nebius tailors optimizations in Nebius Token Factory, its inference platform, to specific customer’s specific goals, whether speed, reliability, quality or price.

One recent example of how they do this is speculative decoding, which allows smaller models to predict likely next tokens that a larger model verifies in bulk, rather than generating one token at a time. Nebius uses each customer’s own traffic to improve the result.

NVIDIA, meanwhile, is helping companies avoid unnecessary compute altogether. A feature in its Dynamo platform locates already-computed data sitting in a cluster’s KV cache so teams don’t waste compute recalculating it.

“We’re seeing a lot of bang for the buck in terms of driving performance, efficiency and overall effectiveness,” noted NVIDIA’s Dion Harris.

Uber has seen its token costs stabilize in recent months even as its use of agentic workflows has grown, said Mattie Toia. She credited caching pushed down to individual sub-agents, plus a simpler shift: giving engineers visibility into their own usage.

“It starts by giving visibility to individual users—how many tokens they’re spending, the relative cost of them. That gives people context to think about how they’re optimizing,” she said.

Boroditsky described the shift as moving from “token maxing” to “value maxing”: measuring how many agent turns, tokens and dollars it takes to reach an outcome, whether that’s a document or a completed form.

“What you’re looking for is, how do I actually optimize the value that I’m creating for the cost that I’m spending?” he said.

The ecosystem at work

Improving the economics of compute is a job for the whole industry, not any one company, the panel agreed. “It takes a lot more than a chip to deliver AI at scale,” Harris said.

He pointed to compounding gains from pairing new hardware with better software—kernel tuning, smarter frameworks, and tools built across NVIDIA’s ecosystem. Over a chip’s lifetime, this can drive 3-5X performance gains from day zero to year five.

Boroditsky added that no single model wins every use case.

“Models matter a lot, but by themselves, they don’t solve a problem,” he said. “It’s the entire end-to-end solution.”

Data discipline

One thing companies can do today, Toia said, is get their own data in order.

“There is a lot of valuable data that most organizations have that is really important to grounding your models,” she said. Uber built an internal “context graph”—roughly 24 million nodes pulled from Jira tickets, system design docs and code reviews—to feed its AI agents better context, cutting query times from 20 minutes to 30 seconds while using fewer tokens.

Boroditsky agreed with this approach, noting that the companies that build centralized resources get better results. His five-year prediction: “The leading companies in the market will have taken control of their intelligence.”

The future of pricing

Asked whether Nebius would consider outcome-based pricing, Boroditsky said the company was open to the idea.

“I don’t think we’ve figured out yet the right economic model between the supplier and the customer,” he said.

Nebius already runs capacity auctions and recently launched spot pricing. As the applications built on Nebius move toward outcome-based models, Boroditsky noted that vendors will have to adapt. Looking ahead, he expects managed services to route workloads intelligently on customers’ behalf.

“In the coming quarters, you’re going to see a lot more managed services that are doing more of the heavy lifting,” he said.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Partner Content
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: AI Agenda Live: From Token Maxing to Value maxing: Getting More From Every Unit of Compute

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
For years, deep-pocketed venture firms have partnered with seed investors to get access to startups’ later rounds if their growth takes off. The bigger firms often invest in the seed funds, with a handshake agreement that they’ll get a heads-up if a hot young startup is about to raise again. 

A firm called Megalith, which has kept a low profile until now, is carving a different path to investing in the most promising young startups and compensating the seed funds for their discovery. It is targeting what’s known as the pro rata rights that an investor gets when first investing in a portfolio company, entitling it to invest in future rounds to avoid dilution of its stake. Megalith offers to take the seed funds’ pro rata allocation or other follow-on investments.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Dealmaker
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Lightspeed’s Top Fundraiser Joins Firm That Takes Seed Funds’ Pro Rata

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
We’re well into the growth-through-acquisition era in the food-delivery industry. Uber’s $2.3 billion purchase of business catering firm ezCater, unveiled on Tuesday, comes just a few weeks after DoorDash snapped up a college campus meal-delivery business for $300 million from Wonder. Neither of these acquisitions will excite many investors, but they signal that Uber and DoorDash are leaving no stone unturned to keep their growth rates humming.

Both companies have been busy consolidating the European food-delivery market, to be sure, buying major players such as Deliveroo and Wolt (for DoorDash) and Delivery Hero (for Uber). But there are only a handful of such companies. And for both Uber and DoorDash—which between them dominate the delivery of restaurant meals and, increasingly, groceries and the like—growth by signing up new subscribers can only get harder.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: The Briefing
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Uber's M&A Blitz

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
This July, Nvidia caught wind of a looming takeover of OpenRouter, a three-year-old startup that had emerged as a popular marketplace for AI models, including many cheaper open-source ones. Databricks and Stripe had already been talking to the startup about a potential sale. Nvidia was late to the party. The chipmaker’s CEO, Jensen Huang, wanted in.

Nvidia executives told their counterparts at OpenRouter they were interested and were prepared to make a generous offer, but they needed more time to evaluate a possible transaction before doing so, said a person with knowledge of the discussion. OpenRouter’s founders didn’t want to wait. Ultimately, Nvidia—whose interest in the startup hasn’t previously been reported—didn’t make a formal offer, and Stripe prevailed with an $8 billion bid for OpenRouter.

Nvidia’s dealmakers quickly moved on to other prizes. Over the next two months, they inked more than $140 billion worth of deals—including a $105 billion credit guarantee. The company held nearly $100 billion worth of equity investments and $25 billion in future investment commitments as of late July. More deals are likely.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Where Nvidia’s $100 Billion Dealmaking Juggernaut Will Go Next

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Ashish Kumar, a former AI lead for Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robots, has co-founded a startup developing non-humanoid robots that handle a variety of tasks that would normally be done by highly skilled workers in industries such as manufacturing and aerospace, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. 

The San Francisco startup, Intelligent Machines, has hired several former members of Tesla’s Optimus team and is in the process of raising a seed round that could end up around $100 million, said one of the people.

Intelligent Machines is currently focused on developing software for robots, but its leaders have discussed designing the hardware as well. 

The company uses reinforcement learning—a method that rewards AI for accomplishing certain goals and penalizes it for other actions—to teach robots to perform complex tasks, according to the two people. (Kumar’s doctoral research at the University of California, Berkeley, focused on RL.)
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: AI Agenda
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Former Tesla Optimus Lead is Launching an Industrial Robot Startup

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Earlier this year, officials at Mississippi electric utility Entergy had some worrisome news for Amazon: It was going to have to start kicking the company’s Mississippi-based data centers off the grid during peak times to ensure it could support other customers, according to two people with knowledge of the situation.

Amazon’s cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, operates one data center near Jackson, Miss., which it is expanding, and it is building two more data center facilities in the same general area, making the state an important region in its data center buildout. Utilities rarely kick off major customers, but Entergy’s message, which hasn’t been previously reported, reflects how soaring demand for power from AI cloud operators is forcing power companies to take unprecedented measures to balance the needs of their various customers.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: How Amazon Rewired Its Data Centers After Mississippi Power Warning

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Sriram Krishnan, a key AI adviser to President Donald Trump who left the White House in June, is raising an AI-focused venture fund, according to three people familiar with the matter. The fund will target raising around $500 million to invest in growth- and later-stage companies, the people said.

Before joining the Trump administration, Krishnan worked for tech companies including Microsoft and Twitter. He later became a general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, where he helped launch the venture firm’s London office. At the White House, Krishnan worked under AI and crypto czar David Sacks on the administration’s AI policy, helping to spearhead its AI action plan, released in July 2025.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Ex-Trump AI Adviser Sriram Krishnan Targets Raising a $500 Million Venture Fund

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
The investing frenzy in data centers that the AI boom sparked has created a bargain-hunting opportunity—in everything but AI assets.

AI has pulled investors’ attention away from unglamorous assets in sectors like transportation and waste management over the past few years, as they have poured billions into data centers and related AI infrastructure. Now investors are getting excited about boring-sounding assets that can throw off cash, like landfills or rail terminals. 

And while mega-investments have become the norm in building massive AI data centers, investors argue that far smaller but still essential plays like regional airports can offer attractive returns.

“The intense focus on digital infrastructure means that you increasingly have high-quality mature assets in other more traditional parts of the infrastructure ecosystem, whether that's in utilities, transport, social infrastructure and so on, which are receiving less of the spotlight,” said Nicholas Pepper, a managing director at the infrastructure business of Partners Group, an asset manager with $186 billion in AUM at midyear. “This is creating opportunities to acquire these assets at attractive valuations.”

The sheer scale of the capital needed for the AI buildout has pulled unprecedented sums into the infrastructure investing market.Blackstone, for instance, has made AI a major theme across its businesses, including infrastructure, credit, private equity and real estate. And in a landmark deal announced last October, a group of investors, including BlackRock’s Global Infrastructure Partners, acquired Aligned Data Centers at an enterprise value of around $40 billion, the largest such sale at the time.

Partners Group, for its part, which closed its fourth infrastructure-dedicated fund at over $15 billion in July, has itself been among the investors piling into data center infrastructure. Its deals include an initial $1 billion investment in AVK Power Solutions, a power provider for data centers in Europe, announced in August.

But there are growing signs that investors across AI-related assets have grown more selective amid construction delays, rising financing costs and regulatory blowback that could slow the AI buildout or hurt its eventual payoff. Those pressures are showing up in delayed data center developer IPOs and ballooning financing costs, but could also stall the predictable cash flows that make infrastructure investments attractive in the first place.

Meanwhile, though investors’ attention has been on AI, the prospects for more traditional infrastructure generally haven’t suffered too much. That’s a contrast to other asset classes, where areas such as software fell out of favor because investors feared a direct hit to their business from AI.

Infrastructure investors say they’re embracing traditional assets in transportation and logistics, aviation, waste and water infrastructure, bridge and road maintenance and gas processing, among other sectors, along with the stable cash yields and contracted or regulated revenues that typically come along with them.

And investors more focused on middle-market deals argue they’re particularly well positioned because the biggest infrastructure investors have gravitated toward the AI sector, leaving smaller transactions with less competition.

“U.S. mega cap investors’ minimum check sizes have gotten so big that they won't come down and participate in this segment of the market, so it has created a huge economic moat for us,” said Brett Stevenson, a founder and managing partner at Canadian private equity and infrastructure investment firm BTG Capital.

While BTG has sold several power facilities to data centers, benefiting from the boom in some ways, most of its investments have been focused on transportation and logistics, as well as energy and utility assets that weren’t a data center play. For instance, the firm in June acquired the then-closed Stephenville International Airport with plans to restore and modernize the Newfoundland-based airport’s infrastructure, and reopened it on Oct. 2. Assets like airports are in a “very scarce asset class, and obviously scarcity can drive potential multiple arbitrage in the future,” Stevenson said.

Larger investment firms have also been active in less glamorous corners of infrastructure. Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners, which has made a number of data center investments, is zeroing in on the waste management sector due to the stability offered by its long-term municipal contracts, low exposure to commodity risk and geopolitical tensions and growth opportunities in regions looking to reduce landfill reliance, said a person familiar with the matter.

U.S. waste management companies in particular command a premium and are currently trading at a valuation of around 15 times Ebitda versus 10 times Ebitda for European companies, the person said. U.S. companies tend to control more of the waste process, integrating everything from garbage pickup to treatment facilities and landfills where it winds up.

Meanwhile, the broader transportation sector also offers more cyclical infrastructure bets that could be poised for an upswing. That includes in the freight and U.S. trucking sectors, which had been grappling with overcapacity following a pandemic-era boom, as well as higher fuel and other operating costs.

The sector is also grappling with geopolitical tensions, which can disrupt shipping routes, pushing valuations down across the broader transportation and logistics sector. That all means a potentially attractive entry point for infrastructure investors, which often compete with strategic buyers for certain assets like ports and rail terminals. The median Ebitda multiple for strategic deals in the broader transportation and logistics space dropped to 5 times in the first quarter of this year from 12.7 times in 2025, according to a report from middle-market investment bank R.L. Hulett.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
A new age of discovery and automation is here. Can you feel it? The leading AI companies certainly can. But you may not.

The rare slow news day gave us more time to marinate on the significance of OpenAI’s late-breaking announcement on Tuesday that its unreleased AI model had solved or made major progress on hundreds of significant problems in math and computer science. What does it mean for those of us who don’t exert much brain power on algebra every day? 

It’s difficult to separate these huge technical achievements from more commercially driven announcements that just keep the AI money train going. And it wasn’t lost on me that Tuesday’s announcement, while groundbreaking, came amid reports of OpenAI raising more cash, and a week after its buzzy developer day mostly underwhelmed. Meanwhile, the latest AI craze—consumer agents—is starting to crash into the reality that a lot of websites want to block bots. And economists don’t see signs yet, at least in major statistics, that AI is making us more productive.

One question animating this phase of the AI gold rush is: How will companies convert raw, impressive intelligence into actual, demonstrable usefulness? 

I witnessed the debate recently at the Midway, a dark auditorium near the San Francisco waterfront that often hosts EDM shows and art exhibitions. Last week, nearly 800 software developers filed inside for a conference hosted by Modal—not an EDM DJ, but a highly valued seller of computing infrastructure and software tools for developers.

Modal gave headline billing to Scott Wu, who used to be best known for his prowess in math competitions, before the coding agent startup he founded, Cognition, rocketed to a $48 billion valuation last month. 

He stood on stage in front of a slide that read: “It’s time to be ambitious.” He talked about a near future where companies are full of “virtual employees,” which would “work on outcomes instead of tasks.” With enough data centers, memory and sandboxes, the industry would get there, he said. “Agents keep getting more and more capable. That’s the entire trend.”

And what gave him confidence for his call to arms was math. “The moment for me was the AIME moment,” he said, referring to the time last year when advanced AI models began reasoning well enough to outperform humans on the kinds of high-level math competitions he used to compete in. “That’s when I knew it was all over”—meaning, humans no longer claim a monopoly on intelligence.

I heard a different tone later that afternoon at the conference from Diogo Almeida, a former OpenAI researcher who described himself as “co-author of some of OpenAI’s greatest hits.” Almeida, smiling and wearing a pink fur coat on stage, spoke with the insider zeal of someone who had defected from a problematic country or religion and could now tell you all about it. He now runs TypeSafe AI, which recently launched a popular alternative to large language models called Jev. 

“Where the fuck is all the automation?” he asked the crowd, before firing off a string of recognizable acronyms, at least to this crowd. “My TL;DR on the state of what is going on in AI is 100% of LLMs today are optimized for assistance with RLHF.” (For the uninitiated, the latter acronym is reinforcement learning from human feedback.) In other words, LLMs are trained to please a human in the loop, so they excel at assistance and fail at unattended automation.

At the same event I heard some of the most important AI leaders pushing for more automation among their software engineering ranks, even as they acknowledged it could be a tough change. They didn’t sound ready to let the machines take over, either. 

“One area we’re pushing a lot more on is [to] think, what are the repetitive tasks I’m doing all the time? Why am I still in that loop?” said Cat Wu, head of product for Claude Code at Anthropic, perhaps the most AI-pilled company in the world. “A lot of automation gets stuck in this stage of being semi-automated. Claude does 80% of the work, and I do 20%. And you’re doing the tasks repetitively.”

And some software engineering leaders are still vexed more by taming humans than AI agents. Dax Raad, a prominent open-source developer who built OpenCode, said his company’s latest problem was that human engineers aren’t actually paying enough attention to code that AI is writing. “I’m just trying to figure out how to get my team to ask the right questions and feel bad when something goes out that they didn’t pay attention to,” Raad said. “It’s the age-old problem: how do you get people to care more?”

In Other News

• Elon Musk announced on Tuesday night that SpaceX’s AI unit will now use some AI models from competitors to power Grok Bot, signaling a shift away from relying exclusively on models developed in-house.

• Microsoft on Wednesday unveiled its latest effort to run AI in PCs powered by its Windows software, rather than running the AI in the cloud, which the company said would bring down costs for customers. More here.

• Anjney Midha, a former general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, along with former executives at Google, Apple and Nvidia have launched a company that aims to make it easier and more affordable for smaller companies or startups to access such compute.

• The U.S. Treasury Department said Wednesday it had fined the parent company of startup accelerator Plug and Play Tech Center, the first penalty issued under an outbound investment restriction program targeting China’s tech sector.

Last month, Zach Dell, son of billionaire Michael Dell and cofounder of Base Power, a billion-dollar battery startup, was gabbing with podcaster David Senra when Senra asked him which of his investors have been the most helpful to him.

Dell’s three-year-old company has many prominent backers, including Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive Capital and angel investor Elad Gil. Dell didn’t name any of them.

“Honestly, our mutual friend Zach,” Dell said.

The other Zach they were referring to was Zach Frankel, 37, a rising star investor who has played an outsized role in building some of tech’s most valuable and buzziest startups—while deliberately remaining anonymous outside of Silicon Valley’s innermost circles. Frankel is so far under the public radar that Dell and Senra even joked about it on the podcast.

Mathematicians are likely feeling the kind of anxiety that software engineers have experienced for months in the wake of OpenAI release on Tuesday of a whopping 722 research papers with AI-created solutions to a range of problems across math subjects. 

AI’s success solving ultra-difficult math problems—even though it still makes mistakes doing simple math—is due to several factors. Solutions to math problems can often be verified, much like software code, and there’s a lot of overlap between mathematics and the work that AI researchers do (and which these researchers are trying to automate in pursuit of RSI).

And with enough computing resources, the AI can essentially do the heavy-duty number crunching that would take humans years to do, and it doesn’t give up. One mathematician who is part of a group advising OpenAI on how to publicly disclose its math breakthroughs told me that they refer to these abilities as brute force and stamina.

Here’s a news flash: The quasi-revenue numbers for OpenAI that got wide circulation last week were off— way off.  Instead of $70 billion in annualized revenue, as we and others reported, OpenAI is generating closer to $50 billion in annualized revenue (sometimes shortened to ARR). A Financial Times report of the lower number on Thursday proved such a shock to investors that stocks of chip firms and neoclouds, including Nvidia, CoreWeave, Nebius and others, fell on the news, CNBC reported.

The cause of this debacle is complicated. But it’s a reminder that we all rely too much on annualized revenue as a way to track a company’s performance. It’s become a standard measure for AI companies because their revenue has been growing by leaps and bounds, making the more common quarterly reports seem a little quaint in their backward-looking nature. But taking one month’s revenue and multiplying it by 12, as is the standard way these annualized-revenue numbers are calculated, is a poor substitute for a fuller picture of a company’s performance. (This isn’t a new issue—see this 2020 story on the subject.)

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
The basement of Gary Flake’s contemporary home in a quiet neighborhood in Bellevue, Wash., is furnished with everything you’d expect in a multipurpose man cave. There’s a cozy-looking couch situated between a large screen and a digital projector, a Peloton treadmill and a rowing machine. The real showpiece of the space, however, is a custom computer that resembles an oversized erector set, one with seven large Nvidia graphics processing units dangling from its frame.

Flake, a former Microsoft executive and startup founder, built the computer to train custom AI models on terabytes of data from electroencephalograms, the tests that measure electrical activity in the brain—part of a startup project he has since moved on from. To train his AI models, Flake could have paid a cloud service to train them on the industrial-strength GPUs inside their data centers, but he said it was far cheaper to assemble his own machine out of discounted parts (total cost: under $6,000) than to fork over fees to Amazon Web Services or Microsoft every month.

That’s true even when including the $10,000 to $20,000 he spent for electrical upgrades and a new HVAC system he bought to keep his basement cool while his AI computer throws off a lot of heat. “I want to own,” said Flake, who plans to begin using the computer again for a new AI project in the coming months. “I don’t want to rent.”

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
• The Big Read: Meet Zach Frankel, the secretive investor behind Cognition, Ramp

• Why techies are hoarding AI compute in their homes

• Plus, Recommendations—our weekly pop culture picks: “Bram Stoker’s Dracula,” “The AGI Chronicles” and “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother”

Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and CEO of Meta Platforms, was only six years old in 1990, the year the Human Genome Project got launched.

That project, a multibillion-dollar international effort led by the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy, resulted in the announcement 10 years later of an awe-inspiring milestone: the first sequencing of the human genetic code—the building blocks of life. When President Bill Clinton described the achievement in 2000, he framed it in grand terms: “We are learning the language in which God created life.”

So it was intriguing to hear another scientific collaboration compared to that earlier achievement at a reception this week hosted by Biohub, the primary philanthropic effort of Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan. The event this week is one of a number of recent moments that herald a changing of the scientific guard from major universities to big tech companies.  

Speaking at the Treehouse Hotel in Sunnyvale, Calif., Zuckerberg told the gathering of around 100 tech executives, scientists and academics that he and Chan had started the first version of what is now called Biohub almost 10 years ago to the day with the goal of trying to cure and prevent all diseases by the end of the century. “We got a lot of eye rolls,” Zuckerberg said. “People thought that was kind of crazy.” Thanks to AI and other advances in technology, he added, “That no longer seems quite so crazy.”

He then turned to Lori Goler, president of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, who announced that Biohub is partnering with the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy in a $1.8 billion investment to create new technologies and build the scientific infrastructure required to drive “AI-powered biology.” 

Biohub, which launched what it calls the “Virtual Biology Initiative” in April with a $500 million commitment, also said at the event that Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, a company spun off of DeepMind, have agreed to kick in $300 million.

“We were inspired by the Human Genome Project,” Goler told the group. Goler added that they hope the initiative “will have the same level of impact and will be as important as the Human Genome Project has been.” (Anyone going to The Information’s WTF Summit later this month will hear more from Goler on the future of AI biology.)

Despite the evening’s focus on collaboration, science can be an isolating discipline in its daily practice. When I visit labs, I am always amazed by how quiet they are. The scientists are usually intently concentrating on not making a false step that could lead to the contamination of an experiment. And yet, once the results leave the lab and reach the public, clamor often ensues. Controversial findings spark debate over ethical and moral questions. Transformative discoveries are celebrated with an element of pageantry and recognition. Both are reminders of our common humanity—and that the ultimate goal of science is to make all our lives better. This leads to invitations to the White House like the one that happened back in 2000 with the scientists at the helm of the Human Genome Project. Or even more personal celebratory videos like the ones posted on social media all this week by happy scientists who received early morning calls from Sweden learning they had won Nobel Prizes. (How can you not be moved by this video of the Stanford neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth telling his kids he won the Nobel Prize for medicine?)

Zuckerberg is one of the most prominent symbols of how AI is altering the scientific landscape and bringing new leaders into an arena once dominated by major universities.  He was appointed by President Trump in March to be a member of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He is joined there by other high-profile Silicon Valley names, including Google’s Sergey Brin, Oracle’s Larry Ellison and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. Of the 13 people now on the council, only one is an academic researcher.

Two other signs this week reflect the change. On Oct. 8, Brin and Huang, alongside other tech notables, received the National Medals of Science from President Trump. The same day, Anthropic said it is expanding its own partnership with the government. It will provide $150 million worth of AI credits and other support for the Genesis Mission launched by Trump last year to use AI to accelerate scientific discoveries.

A Biohub team traveled to Washington in July to attend the first Genesis Mission Summit. Plans for the newly announced partnership with the National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy grew out of that visit. So perhaps it’s only fair that the government made its own pilgrimage out to Silicon Valley. Appearing on stage together is another way of showing a shared faith that Silicon Valley and AI are the favored engines these days to try to unlock insights into the mysteries of our cells and what goes wrong when we get sick.

I talked briefly with Goler the day after the reception. She said Biohub plans to host an annual AI and bio event. Biohub will likely find more guests eager to attend, from the private sector and the government. “It really is a cultural moment,” she said.—Amy Dockser Marcus (amy.marcus@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Bram Stoker’s Dracula”

How do you give, uh, fresh life to Bram Stoker’s classic? Filling it up with an all-star cast of film actors sure works. In Audible’s new adaptation of “Dracula,” Jonathan Bailey is the undead count; Maggie Gyllenhaal is Van Helsing, the occult expert who leads the expedition to destroy the vampire; and Ella Purnell (from “Fallout” and “Yellowjackets”) is Mina, a character reimagined from Stoker’s original from hapless victim into the story’s central protagonist. 

Thanks to its Amazon budget, Audible clearly spared no expense: the sound production is top-notch and directing duties of the audio dramatization went to Mary Lambert, a Hollywood veteran best known for her 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King’s “Pet Sematary.” —Abram Brown

Reading: “The AGI Chronicles” by Kevin Roose

How exactly did we get here—to this moment in time with AIs that increasingly seem human absolutely everywhere? And that’s to say nothing of the endless hand-wringing about whether they’re actually going to end all of us humans. 

A rather definitive answer to that question lies in “The AGI Chronicles,” a colorful, insidery account of the tech industry’s rapacious quest to develop artificial general intelligence. Or, as author Kevin Roose terms it, “the strangest decade in our history.” Roose, the former New York Times technology columnist, begins in the 2010s, a period when creating human-like AI was seen as something “between a pipe dream and a fantasy,” he writes, though a few people who are now bold-faced names wanted to give it a shot: OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis among them. Of course, what looked like a quixotic endeavor then quickly morphed into the multitrillion-dollar competition that currently surrounds us. 

As Roose charts the twists and turns, he includes many little details to love. Just before Altman, Oracle’s Larry Ellison and President Donald Trump announced Project Stargate in January 2025, Altman had to send a last-minute text message to Jeff Bezos to make sure they could use that name for their massive data center initiative: Bezos’s Amazon owns MGM, and MGM owns the rights to the “Stargate” TV-and-movie franchise. Meanwhile, Google’s Gemini was almost called Titan—a Hassabis suggestion—but company lawyers vetoed the name as “too aggressive.” And when Daniela Amodei worked at OpenAI, she and her husband, an early OpenAI board member, used a large collection of stuffed animals as their “personal advisory council,” as Roose puts it. (That detail went viral a bit last week from an early excerpt of the book.) 

From “The AGI Chronicles,” what I was struck by most is how the AI race has warped its contestants and magnified their worst tendencies. I expect that trend will continue. It’s not as if they’ll be facing any less pressure anytime soon. According to Roose, many of those titans echoed the same sentiment in conversations with him—that they “missed their old lives, and they relished the times when everyone thought they were crazy for believing that AGI was possible,” he writes. “Being an underdog, they said, was more fun than being a power broker, with all the scrutiny and skepticism it brought.”—A.B.

Watching: “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother”

By actor Mahershala Ali’s own telling, the past few years have been challenging, with his fate skewed by other forces that have defied his control, including Marvel’s decision to shelve his reboot of “Blade,” its half-vampire vampire slayer. 

“I think in some ways I’m probably just now starting to let certain things go, because there are ways in which I think I’ve begun to let go of my expectations of the world and the business,” Ali said in a recent GQ interview to promote his new film, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.” “It’s like you’re fighting with people to see you how you see yourself.”

I can see how Ali’s own real-life wrestling with his identity and fate might’ve fueled his interest in doing “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.” His character in the film, a mournful hitman named Latif, faces those same challenges—as he tries to extricate himself from a dingy Houston underworld and take up single-parent duties to his three children. Complicating that escape is a gangster pastor (John Cho) and his mobster former employer (Laith Nakli). The thriller-ish drama is punctuated by several balletic action sequences, all deftly handled by newcomer director Bassam Tariq, who’d been attached to helm the “Blade” reboot with Ali. If nothing else, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” is a sharp jab to Marvel’s ribs: Tariq and Ali seem like they would’ve made a terrific “Blade” together.—A.B.

Companies have spent the past few years figuring out how to put AI to work. In 2026, some are confronting a bigger question: What should a company look like when AI can understand context, coordinate work and act across systems?

The Information’s Co-Executive Editor Amir Efrati sat down with leaders from three companies at the forefront of this shift to discuss how agentic AI is changing how companies work and operate.

  • Owen Jennings, Business Lead & Executive Officer, Block
  • Stephanie Cohen, Chief Strategy Officer, Cloudflare
  • Surabhi Gupta, CTO, Klaviyo

Redesigning the operating model

Block and Cloudflare offered two ways to rethink the operating model. For Cloudflare, Stephanie Cohen said the company had to rethink the work itself, not simply add AI tools onto existing processes.

“If we didn’t redesign how work was done, we weren’t going to actually change what went on at Cloudflare,” she said. “The only way for us to redesign the factory floor was to get rid of whole functions.”

At Block, the answer was to rebuild its functional model so engineering, product, design and sales teams work across Square, Cash App and Afterpay on shared capabilities. Owen Jennings said the change came about when AI agents became capable of writing production code in complex systems, prompting the company to ask how work should move when agents can share company context with humans.

“We said, based on where the tools are now and based on where we think it’s going, what functions do we need at the company? How do we want to organize?” recalled Jennings.

The shift is showing up in customer experiences, with Square and Cash App surfacing tools, insights or actions at the right moment, rather than relying on static, one-size-fits-all surfaces. Block shipped about three times as many Square features in the first half of 2026 as a year earlier, he said.

“There’s a lot of conversation around automating things for the sake of it,” said Jennings. “For us, it’s about building useful stuff for customers.”

Humans still matter

Companies leaning hardest into agents aren’t necessarily trying to replace humans. Cloudflare hired 1,111 interns this year, including AI-native talent who Cohen said worked on “everything,” including old-fashioned automation no one had made time to build.

“By teaching them the company and allowing them to have access to our system, they’ve shown us a million ways that what we were doing didn’t make sense,” she said.

Block has also built a workspace for working alongside agents. Buzz, an open source tool the company has released for people and AI agents, gives each agent its own identity, permissions and context.

“The idea is not to remove people from the loop, but to make agent work visible and steerable so humans can focus on judgment, taste and customer understanding,” Jennings said.

Klaviyo wants engineers closer to customer outcomes rather than assigned tickets.

“One of the things we’ve found very effective is having the engineers sit side-by-side with the partner functions, and have them become domain experts,” said Klaviyo’s Surabhi Gupta.

Cloudflare runs hands-on workshops that are deliberately low-pressure, and names an AI “champion” on each team, typically someone already experimenting.

“It’s easier to ask a peer than to ask someone else who you feel like is not gonna understand why you don’t know how to do everything,” Cohen said.

Companies also need infrastructure connecting agents to systems, data and context. Cohen described Cloudflare’s approach as a “harness”: a layer connecting AI models with security, systems of record, company context and employee identities, while letting the company switch models as needed.

“Part of the problem is people started with the hammer and were like, ‘here’s this hammer, build this house.’ The reality is you have to design the house,” said Cohen.

The new metrics

Agentic AI is also creating new metrics to measure success. At Block, development velocity—the pace that new features are shipped—has become a key metric. Gupta says Klaviyo measures this too, as well as cost and hours saved as a result of agents.

One metric no one on the panel could predict: headcount, though Cohen felt optimistic about growth.

“My guess is we’ll have more employees [in five years],” she said. “The human world is human-shaped, and humans want to interact with more humans.”

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Rebuilding Companies for the Agentic Era

If it’s Monday, it must be time for another AI model release. This time, it was Meta Platforms’ turn, unveiling Muse Wonder, which it claims can “deliver state-of-the-art performance” on certain tasks. It was a triumphant moment for the company, whose AI efforts previously went through a slump that prompted a massive hiring binge over the past 14 months or so. That would be notable if only everyone wasn’t claiming to be doing the same thing. Two weeks ago, Google unveiled its latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, which it says “delivers frontier performance in complex workflows” across various subjects (you wouldn’t want it to deliver frontier performance in simple workflows, would you?). In early September, OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which it said was “state of the art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science and professional work.” Also in September, Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, which it claimed to be “the world’s most advanced models for coding and knowledge work.”
