tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Meta Reaches AI’s Crowded Frontier—Will Users Care?

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
To understand the decision-making of AI, developers often look at the text that models produce as they reason through problems. But these “chains of thought” are increasingly hard to read, which is prompting AI developers to consider other approaches. One alternative, known as “mechanistic interpretability,” seeks to explain the inner workings of AI models, rather than just relying on their outward behavior.

Leading AI companies have formed mechanistic interpretability teams in recent years, and the field has spawned several startups, the most prominent of which is Goodfire AI, whose chief scientist Tom McGrath joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. (The full episode is available here.)
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: TITV
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Researchers Need to Learn How AI Makes Decisions, Says Goodfire’s Tom McGrath

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
OpenAI is grappling with fallout from its use of a controversial innovation in AI design as it works to get its next unreleased model to a place where leaders believe they can safely release it.

The model design, known as loop transformers or recurrent depth, can make it harder to monitor the way the AI “thinks,” or how it reasons and processes its response to a question or task, The Information reported last month. That means the technique could erode a key tool that OpenAI and other companies rely on to catch misbehaving models. OpenAI hasn’t publicly acknowledged the technique, but Microsoft last week accidentally confirmed OpenAI’s use of it in one of the AI company’s most advanced commercially available models, GPT-6.1 Sol, in a blog post it has since edited to remove the disclosure.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: OpenAI Scrambles to Fix Safety Issues Before Shipping Its Next Flagship Model

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Neoclouds and so-called inference providers that help app developers run open source models are trying to differentiate themselves in a very crowded market. 

For instance, one such neocloud, Prime Intellect, which was valued at $1 billion in an equity financing in July, is buying a startup to help it make open models run faster and more cheaply on its Nvidia servers, compared to its rivals.  

Prime Intellect, based in San Francisco, is acquiring Moondream, a young developer of open-source models that has fewer than 10 employees, according to Prime Intellect co-founder and CEO Vincent Weisser. (Weisser wouldn’t share the terms of the deal, but Moondream has raised $4.5 million in funding.) 

San Francisco- and Seattle-based Moondream is best known for an open-source vision-language model for analyzing and understanding images, like identifying boxes in an image of a warehouse or ads in a livestream. But Prime Intellect is largely acquiring the startup for its employees’ skills in writing software to make models run more efficiently, Weisser said.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: AI Agenda
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Neocloud Prime Intellect Acquires Startup To Speed Up Inference

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
The trillion-dollar question of the AI boom is whether businesses’ spending on the technology pays off. But measuring that return is often uncertain, confusing or incomplete. 

That’s because it takes time for AI to show a return on investment that can be demonstrated in a company’s income statement, as we’ve written.

A new study from the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School and GBK Collective, a consultancy, echoes this idea, showing that most companies are still tracking ROI by measuring whether it makes their workers more efficient rather than whether it is driving more revenue. The study, based on online surveys of 1,400 U.S.-based employees from firms that have at least 1,000 staff and generate more than $50 million annually, showed that 40% of managers measured AI’s impact on their business in terms of “hours saved per employee” and 37% tracked how AI reduced their workers’ errors. 

Only about 27% of managers said they track the revenue they generate from AI features, apps and tools they provide to their customers.

Perhaps worryingly, 44% of managers said that over the next one to two years, AI’s primary role will be to improve productivity and just 8% said it would be to drive new revenue or create new products.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Applied AI
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Why Companies Can't Prove Their AI Spending Pays Off

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Microsoft has discussed making significant cost reductions in its Azure cloud-server-rental unit, according to a person with direct knowledge of the situation. Girish Bablani, president of Azure, in recent weeks told senior leaders in his group, which has about 11,500 employees, to come up with ideas to reduce costs at least 20%, though it isn’t clear if such a reduction would include layoffs, according to the person.

The discussion comes even as Azure’s revenue growth has accelerated, a sign of how heavily Microsoft’s data center spending is weighing on its finances.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Microsoft Cloud President Asks Leaders to Find 20% Cost Cuts

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Smith + Howard, an accounting firm backed by private equity giant TPG that has grown in part by snapping up smaller firms, is gearing up for a new round of acquisitions—including two that could close by the end of the year. As it grows, the firm is exploring how AI could handle basic work where there’s “a lot of lather, rinse, repeat,” CEO Sean Taylor said.

The firm is hoping AI will help it expand without having to hire accountants at the same pace it did previously—reflecting a broader bet among private equity firms and AI labs that the technology can help boost profits when consolidating professional services firms.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Inside a TPG-Backed Accounting Firm’s Plans for AI and More Acquisitions

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
OpenAI, which is trying to develop a substantial cybersecurity business, is in early talks to buy Trail of Bits, a firm that finds and fixes vulnerabilities in open-source software, according to people familiar with the matter.

The size of the potential deal couldn’t be learned. OpenAI has sometimes paid in the low hundreds of millions of dollars in the form of stock to acquire small startups, though it sometimes pays less. Discussions are ongoing and the deal could fall apart, said the people.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: OpenAI Eyes Acquisition That Could Boost Cybersecurity Business

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
When is someone going to make a TV show set at OpenAI? It’s got swarms of rogue AI agents causing havoc across the internet, not to mention periodic corporate drama. And today we learned that an OpenAI engineer allegedly planted a “sophisticated recording device” inside a company conference room.

The Justice Department identified the engineer—who has been arrested—as a Saudi national and revealed that the bug was attached to the back of a TV set in a conference room where “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information” were often held. OpenAI is a gift that keeps on giving…to journalists everywhere. (Check out our scoop today about how OpenAI is trying to fix its safety issues).
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: The Briefing
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: OpenAI’s Bug and Bumble’s AI-Powered Exit

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
OpenAI’s release last Tuesday of more than 300 math results it says an internal model solved has sparked concern among some of the world’s leading cryptographers, or experts in encoding information to keep it private and secure. They worry that AI’s continued math advances could find new algorithms that make our current methods of protecting information on encrypted services, from online payments to messaging platforms like WhatsApp, easier to crack.

The basis for modern internet security is the assumption that some math operations are easy to do, such as a process of encoding using a number known as the public key. But they are hard to undo, or decode, without knowing a specific number, called the private key. This assumption of difficulty is the foundation of secure communication over the internet, which has helped enable e-commerce, cryptocurrencies and digital accounts.

AI models from OpenAI and others, which have been solving problems that have stumped math experts for decades, have raised the prospect that powerful AI systems could find ways to solve those problems without that key.

“I am anticipating a vast change in mathematics, cryptanalysis included,” said Whitfield Diffie, who helped invent public key cryptography in 1976 with the Diffie-Hellman key exchange algorithm, in an email to me.

“I don’t know the timescale. A year is probably too soon; five may not be,” said Diffie, now a consulting scholar at the Stanford Center for International Security and Cooperation.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: AI Agenda
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: OpenAI’s Math Breakthroughs Rattle Cryptography Leaders

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Anthropic reported rapid-but-slowing revenue growth in a meeting with potential investors in its planned initial public offering, leaving some attendees expecting the company will need to keep its valuation target in check.

At a private investor meeting Wednesday in San Francisco, the company said revenue hit $16.8 billion in the third quarter, according to people briefed on the numbers. That was a jump of about 45% from the second quarter. The figure was more than 3.6 times the company’s revenue for all of 2025. But it also represents a slower growth rate than Anthropic’s second quarter, when fevered demand for its Claude Code product drove revenue up by more than 140% from the first three months of the year.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Artificial Intelligence
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Anthropic’s Rapid But Slowing Growth Could Weigh on IPO Valuation

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
This was not the day to be a publicly traded neocloud (as young AI data center firms are known). As the market sold off on bad inflation data—reinforcing certainty of another interest rate hike—neoclouds tanked. These companies typically are borrowing a lot to finance expansion. The worst hit in the stock sell-off was CoreWeave, whose stock fell 15.5%, fueled by chatter that its bonds were falling to worryingly low levels. 

CoreWeave CEO and co-founder Michael Intrator was defiant. He told his staff, according to a spokesperson: “When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally.” Yeah, right. The issue may be more that Intrator doesn’t understand investors. He sold CoreWeave stock every week between April and the end of September, securities filings show, while his fellow co-founders have also been selling regularly. That can’t help but undermine investor confidence in the company. Intrator could win some brownie points by pledging to stop selling his stock for a while.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: The Briefing
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: CoreWeave Co-Founders’ Stock Sales Aren’t Helping Investor Confidence

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
In the weeks before SpaceX’s AI unit in August introduced Grok Bot, its version of a personal AI agent, engineers at Cursor discovered a potential problem.

Cursor, the AI coding startup SpaceX was then in the process of acquiring, was developing Grok Bot, and as part of that process, employees across Cursor were using the tool extensively for testing and as a part of their everyday work. In late July, engineers raised concerns that Cursor might have sent data from that internal testing—potentially including confidential information about its customers, suppliers and business partners—to SpaceX’s AI unit. One of Cursor’s lawyers warned that if word got out that the company was using the data for training, that could cause a “huge trust problem,” according to internal communications viewed by The Information.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Cursor Staff Investigated Whether Confidential Data Reached SpaceX for AI Training

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
DayOne Data Centers, a Singapore-based data center operator gearing up for a multibillion-dollar initial public offering in New York, is little known to most U.S. investors. But its business is built on a much better known company: ByteDance.

The TikTok parent company accounts for nearly 70% of DayOne’s revenue, according to two people with knowledge of DayOne’s operations. DayOne, which started as a Chinese data center company’s overseas business unit four years ago, has benefitted greatly from ByteDance’s rapid global expansion through TikTok. But that has also left it extraordinarily dependent on a single customer, which the company has acknowledged creates a significant risk for its business.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Singapore’s DayOne Pushes Ahead With Data Center IPO Tied to TikTok

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
To rein in AI spending, large companies are capping employees’ usage, turning to cheaper and smaller models and using routers to send only the hardest requests to the most expensive models.

Cognition, the startup behind the AI coding agent Devin, is adding a new trick to the book: measuring how efficiently different engineers use AI so companies can allocate more resources toward their most efficient employees, Cognition told The Information exclusively.

“The limits that a user should have should not be static. They should be dynamic based on the efficiency of your usage and the value that you're getting out of it,” said Calvin Giroud, a vice president of customer engineering at Cognition.

By looking at an engineer’s coding session using Devin, Cognition can estimate the equivalent number of hours it would have taken a human to do the same amount of work. Dividing by the costs of that session, Cognition gets a measure of each engineer’s efficiency.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: AI Agenda
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Cognition’s Plan to Limit Tokenmaxxing to the Most Efficient Engineers

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
As OpenAI has jockeyed with Anthropic to win over developers with new models and tools this year, its advertising business at times has seemed like an afterthought. Not anymore.

Over the last few months, the company has unleashed a flurry of new products and tools to court advertisers, even as it has cut ad rates. That’s helped lure a lot more advertisers, new data show. The company has also gone on a hiring spree. Nearly half of the roughly 140 OpenAI employees working on ads joined between July and September, according to Crustdata, which tracks employees’ public profiles. Meta Platforms, where ad chief Dave Dugan spent 12 years, is the biggest source of talent.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: OpenAI Accelerates Ad Sprint With Meta Hires, Slashed Prices

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
As companies create more applications using AI, corporate officers say demand is rising for a new type of software that stress-tests those apps, simulating how they handle network problems and other disasters that humans may not think to test for—including cyberattacks by rogue AIs.

Luis Chávez, CTO of coding assistant provider Replit, says his company uses an AI-assisted software known as a deterministic simulator, a kind of flight simulator for software. The deterministic part refers to how the simulator lets companies run the same disaster test again and again so they can try out different fixes for bugs that crop up during network failures or hacking attempts.

Traditional stress-testing methods rely on developers guessing every potential problem that may arise. Merely using today’s AI models to evaluate code often produces false alarms or fake warnings, corporate executives say.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Applied AI
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Why AI-Written Software Needs a Flight Simulator

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
As the U.S. Department of Justice negotiates a settlement of its antitrust lawsuit against Apple, app developers are fretting that any deal won’t go far enough in curbing what they see as Apple’s anticompetitive behavior, according to people familiar with the talks.

Several developers, including PayPal and Epic Games, have discussed their concerns with the Justice Department about a possible settlement of the Apple case, the people said. In communication with developers, Justice Department officials have signaled their preference to settle the lawsuit rather than fight it, the people said.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Apple’s Antitrust Settlement Talks Spur Worries Among Developers

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
It’s beginning to look like Anthropic waited too late to go public. Third-quarter revenue numbers disclosed to investors on Wednesday implied that its growth has slowed from the second quarter, which we reported is likely to put a ceiling on its IPO valuation. Anthropic might have been better off going public in June, when its growth was still spectacular. (Of course, a June IPO might have been impractical given that that’s when SpaceX went public.)

As things stand now, Anthropic’s slowing growth may remind investors of a longstanding question surrounding the company: How much of a moat does it really have? Yes, its AI models are as good as they get, but increasingly, businesses don’t need really expensive frontier models. As we wrote earlier this week, developers are increasingly opting for other models that are good enough for most tasks. Anthropic’s aggressive pricing has prompted companies such as Microsoft to cut its spending on the former’s models, we reported 10 days ago. (This trend seems to be spreading).
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: The Briefing
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Did Anthropic Miss Its Peak IPO Moment?

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
I am thrilled to announce three major editorial promotions for Nick, Abe and Meredith, along with some changes that recognize the incredible work of our newsroom and set the stage for more growth in what is shaping up to be the most exciting time in our history.

Nick Wingfield has been promoted to Executive Editor, responsible for ensuring the high bar of all our reporting. Since he joined The Information eight years ago after working at the New York Times and Wall Street Journal, Nick has pushed us to think bigger in our journalism, overseeing our features efforts and some of our most important beats. When we heard whispers that Jony Ive’s personal life was becoming a distraction from his work at Apple, he and Aaron Tilley mustered a slew of reporting that turned into one of our most memorable crash leders. That’s what he has done again and again. Working with talented reporters to drive maximum impact, across coasts, beats and more.

In his new role, Nick will run the day-to-day publication with me and Amir, with us all dividing up responsibilities for what we chase and ensuring the highest bar in what we publish while continuing to grow the team and build up new editorial areas. He will continue to manage his team of reporters.

Abe Brown has been promoted to Features Editor, with responsibility for all our features at The Information. As Weekend editor, Abe has proven himself as something rare in media these days: a careful and skilled editor with a zest for trying new things. While managing a section, he has also jumped in any day of the week to help edit our biggest stories with a tireless work ethic and great attitude. I am excited for more reporters to work with Abe and for him to push us in new directions.

I am thrilled to promote Meredith Mazzilli to Finance Editor. From the day she joined The Information, it has been clear that Meredith knows finance. While she has led all sorts of consequential coverage on ads, commerce, Musk and beyond, in recent months, she has helped our finance team carve out a huge lane around the financing of data centers and this turbulent moment. I’m excited to see how far she and the team can run against that massively important story. Meredith has also begun the work of bringing new talent to the team. I am thrilled to have her officially step into the role leading Finance, continuing to expand our reporting staff and find even more lanes where we can dominate.

I am also happy to share that Martin has decided he wants to shift his focus to the Briefing and future related Briefing franchises and will become Editor-at-Large. Over twelve years, Martin has had a hand in every aspect of this business. I am thrilled he will be working with us full-time to focus on writing and how to expand the Briefing franchise, while continuing to coach and advise the newsroom. And there will be more time to celebrate more than a decade of Martin as co-Executive Editor. He will continue to edit The Electric and, in the coming weeks, reporters who report to him will transition to other senior leaders to free him up to go full throttle in his new role.

We are making these changes now to celebrate the success of our incredible editorial leadership team, which remains unrivaled in the industry, and to prepare for the future.

The next few years are going to demand a lot of news organizations. Sweeping changes to how audiences consume news are just beginning and I honestly think most news organizations will have no idea what hit them. Meanwhile, the onslaught of “information,” much of it biased and fake, has only begun.

Our secret sauce—the high impact, ahead-of-the-curve, focused work no one else is doing—is exactly the right formula for this moment.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: Nick Wingfield Promoted to Co-Executive Editor of The Information

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
The sentiment gap between public and private markets could not be wider right now. Wall Street investors have been increasingly worried about overborrowing by AI-related companies, as evidenced by skyrocketing yields on CoreWeave bonds, a selloff in semiconductor stocks and the yanking of the IPO of Firmus, the Australian data center operator.

Investors in private tech startups are still ebullient, blown away by how fast startups like Fireworks AI have grown. 

This bifurcation was evident to me this week at Morgan Stanley’s annual private tech companies conference. The mutual fund and other investors fanning out across a lush seaside resort in Dana Point, Calif., were aware of the red washing over trading screens. But that didn’t prevent them from rushing to meet the dozens of startup founders there, particularly if they were in the hot defense or inference sectors. 

“You can see there's a stark disconnect between the public markets and the private markets,” said Diana Doyle, Morgan Stanley’s head of technology equity and equity-linked capital markets on the sidelines of the conference.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Dealmaker
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: The Party Is Still Going Strong for Private Tech

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
DeepSeek is working closely with Huawei Technologies to shape the design of future AI chips, two people familiar with the matter said, in a collaboration that could help China build frontier AI models without Nvidia’s technology.

The relationship goes beyond the kinds of conversations companies have with chip suppliers about their semiconductor road maps. Huawei engineers are incorporating DeepSeek’s requests and suggestions into design decisions, such as how models calculate and move data between processors, for chips that will come out next year and beyond, the people said. To do this work, the Huawei engineers have been stationed at DeepSeek’s offices for an extended period, one of the people said.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: How DeepSeek Is Shaping Huawei’s AI Chips in a Growing Challenge to Nvidia

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
SpaceX put on a bit of a show for shareholders today—and I’m not referring to the sizzle reel of rocket and space videos it showed on its earnings call. No, the big attention grabber was the update from CEO Elon Musk on the progress of SpaceX’s contemplated merger with Tesla and just how involved—or not involved he is in the whole affair. 

First though, it’s worth mentioning the other big highlight from the call: SpaceX’s booming AI—excuse me, SI—business, a category that includes the company’s X social media service, its Grok Bot agent platform and a cloud infrastructure service it has started to rent to outsiders like Anthropic. The segment is on fire. It saw its third-quarter revenue nearly triple to $7.56 billion, making it the largest business category at SpaceX. And if that wasn’t enough, the SI business swung to an operating profit of $431 million from a $1.26 billion loss in the second quarter. 

SpaceX shares jumped nearly 7% in after-hours trading following the report. 

SpaceX executives made it clear that the big story in its SI (superintelligence) segment is its cloud business. Musk told investors the company’s phone is ringing off the hook with demand from businesses that want to lease SpaceX’s AI compute. “We are hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and by dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute,” Musk said. “We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone.” 

For his part, Bret Johnsen, SpaceX’s chief financial officer, described that demand as “extraordinary” and said at the prices it’s currently charging its cloud customers, SpaceX is “generating a payback in less than a year” on new data centers after it deploys them.

Musk also addressed a question from an investor about his desire to unite SpaceX and Tesla. He said the respective companies have formed special committees to examine a merger, but because he’s CEO of both Tesla and SpaceX, he has needed to recuse himself from those discussions. 

Still, that didn’t stop him from telling everyone listening to the call that he thinks a merger is a grand idea. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining both companies,” he said. 

Musk also stated the obvious caveat: Any deal will still need shareholder approval, and there’s no guarantee they’ll bless it. “I think some people assume a SpaceX-Telsa merger is a certainty,” he said. “I think that would be overstating it.” Nonetheless, Musk’s shareholders tend to be very obedient to him. If the companies decide to move forward with a merger, stay tuned for Musk to start turning up his X megaphone and encouraging them to fall in line.

Netflix’s Sad Trombone

The other shoe just dropped at Netflix. Last than a week after announcing the layoffs of about 1,000 employees, or 6% of the company, Netflix reported its weakest quarterly revenue growth in three years—an 11.8% jump to $12.87 billion in revenue. For a figure lower than that, you have to go all the way back to the third quarter of 2023. It didn’t help that Netflix told investors revenue growth will get even worse in the fourth quarter, estimating 11.5% for that period. The company’s shares fell 5% in after-hours trading. 

The weak third-quarter revenue number wasn’t exactly a surprise; it was slightly better than the growth rate Netflix had told analysts to expect last quarter. But it’s obvious from the heads that have rolled at Netflix over the past week that the company’s CEOs, Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters, aren’t happy with the state of its business. The firings included Bela Bajaria, chief content officer, and David Lin, film chief, a sign that the company wants to reset its approach to movies and series. It's still a powerhouse in living rooms: The new season of “The Diplomat” is back on with a vengeance on my TV set. But Netflix feels like it’s looking for a new act. 

In Other News

  • In a draft IPO prospectus, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of more than $80 billion for the first half of the year, reflecting its accounting for financing agreements, The Wall Street Journal reported. Around a fifth of its $16.3 billion in revenue for the period came from two customers. 
  • Elon Musk ordered the slowdown in a military version of Starlink in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal reported.
  • Salesforce agreed to buy customer engagement platform Braze for roughly $5.66 billion, including debt.
  • Joel Kaplan, Meta Platforms’ chief global affairs officer, plans to leave the company after more than 15 years.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Tech earnings season is back (yes, I know it feels like it never ends). This time, we’ve got a slight twist: Meta Platforms has broken with the pack and is reporting its September-quarter earnings on Wednesday, a week ahead of its big tech counterparts, Google, Microsoft and Amazon. (Apple is even later, on Nov. 2.) By reporting earlier than the others, Meta ensures it will grab more of the spotlight, for better or worse.

Until last week’s market sell-off, Meta had been riding a wave of enthusiasm on Wall Street, thanks to chatter about its Muse personal agent and recently released Muse Wonder AI models. Things changed last week, particularly on Friday, as renewed jitters about the AI expansion tanked most tech stocks. Given Meta’s gargantuan spending on AI development, this week’s update will provide a new test of investor sentiment toward Meta shares.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: The Briefing

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
The Information is pleased to announce new reporters who will carry on the publication’s rich track record of reporting exclusive news on the most important people and companies in business. They’ll report on OpenAI, Google, Asia and finance.

Jemima McEvoy, OpenAI

Jemima McEvoy is changing roles to take on the OpenAI beat.

In just over a year at The Information writing for the Weekend section, Jemima has proven herself to be a resourceful, industrious and sharp-eyed reporter with a flair for colorful features and a knack for breaking news. Her run of illuminating stories includes profiles of Epstein-linked investor Masha Bucher, Midjourney founder David Holz and ultra-secretive investor Zach Frankel. An adept collaborator, she also co-authored great reads on OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife Anna, Sequoia’s leadership duo and Anthropic “first lady” Cami Clark—not to mention The Information’s inaugural 50 Most Influential People in Tech list. And she has helped deliver scoops on Valar Atomics and Shield AI and deconstructed trends such as the rise of padel.

Jemima joined The Information after five years at Forbes, where she made her bones writing about billionaires and their businesses. She has also interned for CBS News and was editor-in-chief of Washington Square News, the independent student newspaper at her alma mater, New York University.

Ryan Barwick, Google

Prior to that, she worked on ByteDance’s LLM training operations in Singapore and spent nearly six years as a correspondent at The Business Times, the premier business publication in Southeast Asia, covering venture capital, tech, and private wealth across the region.

Her journalistic work earned her a Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) Media Award for Excellence in 2024 for the investigation into Singapore’s largest money laundering scandal. How many young AI cloud providers can the market, and Nvidia, support?

That’s one of the big questions after a week in which investors worried about the data center buildout and the risks that its unproven participants, known as neoclouds, are taking. Those risks include loading up on debt (CoreWeave) or trying to go public without much of a track record (Firmus and Nscale). Firmus abruptly pulled its public offering last week while shares of CoreWeave and its smaller rivals fell around 20%. The concerns even hit bigger AI cloud providers like Oracle.

Data center and neocloud executives told me there’s a limit to the number of AI cloud providers that can exist, even if Nvidia provides many of them with investment or backstops.

Welcome, Weekenders!

A song has been stuck on loop in my mind for days now. Yeah, this one. 

C’mon, haven’t you heard the big, brassy James Bond theme playing too? We have an honest-to-goodness spy scandal on our hands! That would be the affair over at OpenAI, where the FBI has arrested a former engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, for allegedly placing a toilet paper–wrapped recording device in a conference room. Why’d he do it? The Justice Department wasn’t explicit in its press release announcing Alfozan’s arrest, though the statement does make sure to prominently describe him as a “national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” implying, obviously, that he was hoping to spy on OpenAI for the Saudis.

I expect a not unsizable part of Silicon Valley experienced some schadenfreude when reading about the turn of events at OpenAI. I’d advise against indulging in that feeling, because when I struck up conversations with a few corporate security consultants and surveillance experts over the last few days, they all echoed the same sentiment: Plenty of companies risk ending up in the same situation—especially as they move quickly in today’s era of frenzied, heightened competition. A discomforting thought, eh?

“Organizations can sometimes be moving so fast that they often don’t understand that there’s an issue associated with somebody until that person’s on board and up to no good,” said Bill Priestap, a former head of FBI counterintelligence who now runs his own security consultancy, Trenchcoat Advisors. “Meaning they’re recruiting, and they’re under such pressure to get the right people and get them on board that in many regards, they end up with a minimal understanding of the people they’re bringing on board.” Well, good thing there hasn’t been an enormous, frantic hiring binge lately. Ha ha ha. 

If you’re starting to feel a little paranoid, I strongly, strongly advise against talking to someone like David Abbott, a San Francisco private detective, to find out how easy it is to bug an office. Such conversations will only further unnerve you—you might end up holding your next board meeting in your home basement, Tony Soprano style—because according to Abbott, it’s pretty darn easy to install a recording device. 

A suitable one can be bought for less than $100. Some of the popular ones resemble phone chargers, which get tucked into a power socket, hidden in plain sight. He’s also seen surveillance devices in fake coffee cups—you know, like the ones that might lie casually around an office—and quite a few in fake smoke alarms. 

More bad news: Should you find such a device, it’s like spotting an ant in your kitchen. One ant suggests the presence of more ants. “If I’m doing a bug sweep, just because I find one does not mean there isn’t a second,” said Abbott. “If you find one, there’s going to be two. If you find two, there’s going to be three. You just keep looking.”

What happened at OpenAI underscores Abbott’s warning. There, Alfozan, the alleged spy, did plant two bugs. Well, he tried to do so. Alfozan, not the sort who seems like he would’ve ever earned double 0 status, had placed another bug in a bag that he then mislaid: He reported it missing and had to go pick it up from the company’s lost and found.

OK, if I’ve spooked the heck out of you, I guess I can offer some solace by pointing you in the direction of Eric and Greg Levesque, whose Salt Lake City–based startup, Strider Technologies, has raised $110 million in the last few years to sell AI-powered software to businesses that monitors email and other internal communications, flagging suspicious behavior and possible espionage attempts. (Yes, the company’s name is a reference to Strider from “The Lord of the Rings,” the nom de cloak of Aragorn, the character Viggo Mortensen plays.) 

“What we’ve found is that companies are not always dealing with trained intelligence operatives. Like, they’re dealing with scientists or legitimate engineers who have been approached or coerced in some form or fashion and are now working on behalf of someone else,” said Greg Levesque. “They can leave a lot of digital exhaust.”—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Reaching Out”

As the pandemic shut down the world in 2020, Sayre Quevedo, then a producer for The New York Times’ “The Daily” podcast, quit his job and headed out to Los Angeles, hoping for a chance at self-reinvention. To cope with those tumultuous times, he decided to pursue a documentary project, recording every phone call. Had nothing else of import happened in his life, Quevedo might’ve wound up with an intriguing time capsule. But something quite unusual did occur: Just months after moving to LA, he and his twin brother, Connor, happened to finally locate their biological father, whom they’d never before met. He worked as a barber—blocks from where Sayre lived. “Reaching Out,” a new podcast co-produced by NPR station KCRW that won a top prize in the Tribeca Festival’s expanded podcast categories, is a starkly intimate account of their journey to meet him and their reconciliation with each other, their lives and what life might’ve been like if their father hadn’t been a total stranger who happened to be just down the street.—Abram Brown

Reading: “Sitcom” by Chuck Lorre and “Emperor of Nothing” by Blake J. Harris

Chuck Lorre, the indefatigable TV showrunner, writer and producer, has kept the masses laughing for years—and years—and years, with a list of hits that includes “Two and a Half Men,” “The Big Bang Theory” and “Dharma and Greg.” Those are sitcoms, a term Lorre acknowledges once made him practically break out in hives, since it was often used to cheapen what he sees as grueling, high-touch art. With spicy good humor, he reclaims the word in his new memoir about his time in Hollywood, “Sitcom.” 

“The truth is, making a live studio audience laugh for twenty-odd minutes every week, for twenty-two weeks, is incredibly hard and unbelievably stressful,” Lorre writes. “If you’re one of those people who insist on labeling all sitcoms as being cheap, juvenile and unsophisticated, well…all I can say is, blow me.”

I’d say “Sitcom” functions as a good primer on managing talent, too, and Lorre attests to having learned the importance of keeping out of the way. “Creativity needs air to breathe,” he writes. To do the opposite risks turning a leader into “one of those plastic bags you get at the dry cleaners that can kill small children.” Lorre also takes the opportunity to set down what he sees as good comedy’s basic tenets and decry the medium’s basest impulse: to write only about stupid people doing stupid things: “A better, perhaps deeper means to achieving laughter involves pain and suffering.”

Such a sentiment is most certainly shared by Larry David of “Seinfeld” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” the subject of “Emperor of Nothing,” a biography that won his reluctant cooperation. (When author Blake J. Harris finally wore David down, Harris received a two-line email from him: “Oh Jesus. If we must.”) As with “Sitcom,” “Emperor of Nothing” charts a remarkable rise across Hollywood from an inauspicious start: Lorre was a wannabe musician before his TV run, while David was a little-known stand-up comic with an unremarkable series of TV writing jobs before co-creating “Seinfeld.”

Like Lorre, David describes the process of penning comedy as an arduous affair. And by David’s own telling, the process of sitting down to write a new “Seinfeld” season would bring on full panic. “That always seemed like a daunting prospect,” he recalled. “Especially because all the good ideas were used up the year before.” Fortunately, David had his friendship with the show’s eponymous star, Jerry Seinfeld, one of many people within David’s orbit who gave interviews for “Emperor of Nothing.” “I would always say, ‘All we have to do is write today,’” Seinfeld said. Or as David recalled: “Jerry always talked me off the ledge.”—A.B.

Watching: “War”

No one does a charming, self-involved cad better than Dominic West, the British character actor who first washed ashore in America as “The Wire”’s Detective McNulty and then again in Showtime’s “The Affair” and in the final two seasons of “The Crown” as Prince Charles. In “War,” HBO’s new high-tension legal drama, he’s tech billionaire Morgan Henderson, a fellow championing a safer, more responsible social media—while embroiled in an increasingly messy divorce from his Hollywood star wife, Carla (Sienna Miller). Much of that mess is Morgan’s own doing: He looks wonderful in his Savile Row trousers—he just has trouble keeping them on. As Morgan and Carla gird for an extended battle, they assemble a posse of cutthroat attorneys, who find their impulsive clients constantly upending their carefully laid strategies. That flock of legal eagles includes a handsome rogue, Johnny (Archie Renaux), a lad from working-class south London who sees a chance to ascend by, uh, redefining zealous representation. Backstabbing and double crosses abound.—A.B.

The Trump administration has opened the door for entrepreneurs to start new banks in the U.S., many funded by venture capital. But there’s a catch for fast-growing newcomers. 

Upstarts like Palmer Luckey’s Erebor Bank, as well as other new entrants like Openreserve and Augustus, will likely have to keep raising money as they grow to maintain the capital cushion they need to satisfy bank regulatory requirements. That’s a contrast to most startups, which use fresh venture money to pay for operating expenses and expand the business. 

Regulators require banks to maintain a capital cushion to absorb potential losses and protect depositors. That cushion is typically measured through a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio, which measures a bank’s capital relative to assets including cash, loans and investments. For instance, a bank subject to a 12% minimum tier 1 leverage ratio needs to maintain at least $12 in capital for every $100 in assets. 

As a bank attracts more deposits, its assets, such as loans, typically grow too, increasing the amount of capital it needs to meet that minimum ratio. Established banks can build up their capital through their profits, but newer banks that aren’t yet profitable have to rely instead on raising fresh equity from investors.

Startup banks have already been raising significant funding to get their businesses off the ground or as deposits grow. 

Erebor Bank is set to raise $1.5 billion in a fresh fundraising round at an $8 billion valuation before the investment, after launching with $625 million in committed capital in February. The fundraising comes as the bank has seen its deposits surge to $7 billion as of the end of September, up from $4 billion at the end of the prior quarter. 

Meanwhile, Openreserve, an a16z crypto-backed bank that raised $25 million in September, said it expects to announce an additional capital raise to meet its regulatory requirements ahead of its planned opening early next year. 

Then there’s Augustus, a startup bank focused on serving fintech companies. It raised $180 million in a Tiger Global Management–led round in July at a $1 billion valuation and expects to open later this year. 

Regulators give capital ratios to each bank based on their assessment of the institution’s business plans and risks. Newly created banks typically face tougher capital requirements than established banks. For the first three years of operation, Erebor and Openreserve must each maintain a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio of 12%, while Augustus faces a 10% minimum. Established banks, by comparison, typically have ratios of between 5% and 6%. 

“There’s no question that the regulators treat de novo banks—new banks—differently than they do well-established banks,” according to Brian Graham, a partner and co-founder at consulting firm Klaros Group who advises clients on bank charter applications. Graham noted that the extra capital requirements typically go away after a bank has been operating for three years.

The upstart banks are generally pursuing relatively new business models or focusing on sectors big banks typically avoid. Erebor Bank, for example, has gained traction in areas prioritized by the Trump administration, such as defense startups and crypto firms, and is expanding in geographies traditional banks typically avoid, including Venezuela and Syria. 

In addition to making minimum capital requirements, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.—a banking regulator—imposed an unusual condition on its approval of Erebor for the deposit insurance program. Under a capital-call provision, Erebor’s investors must contribute additional capital if the bank doesn’t meet its minimum capital requirements, according to a filing. The filing didn’t disclose which investors are required to provide the capital backstop. 

In the meantime, upstart banks that are looking to drive revenue growth from lending rather than fees will likely need to tap investors to build their capital. 

“To the extent the bank’s business model is reliant materially on the balance sheet for revenue and net income, you’re going to need to raise more capital to drive growth,” Klaros’ Graham said. 

Openreserve, for its part, plans to make loans backed by traditional assets and turn them into digital tokens that can trade on blockchain, potentially providing a new source of loans for investors and lenders in the crypto market. For example, it plans to lend businesses money against their trade receivables, turning those assets into digital tokens to make them easier to trade. 

“Our ambition is to be the on-chain GSIB,” referring to a globally systemically important bank, said Dee Choubey, founder and CEO of Openreserve. The bank also plans to issue its own stablecoin and to offer tokenized deposits, digital versions of traditional bank accounts that earn interest. Over time, it aims to provide banking and payment services to other digital banks. 

Augustus plans to focus on helping fintech, crypto and remittance companies move money across borders using both traditional banking systems and stablecoins. That will put it in competition with existing banks like United Texas Bank, which has become dominant in processing dollar payments for overseas crypto exchanges.

“Whenever someone outside the U.S. touches the dollar through a local bank or local fintech, that always has to be facilitated by a U.S. nationally chartered clearing bank, so we provide that service,” said Augustus CEO Ferdinand Dabitz. In Europe, the bank already counts crypto exchange Kraken among its clients. 

Augustus is less focused on activities like lending, however, and has a lower ratio than the other two. The company has raised significantly more than its initial capital requirement, which could lessen the need for more fundraising in the near term. “We are less focused on the credit side as other market participants. We think the clearing side is really where we shine,” Dabitz said.

In the last month, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have released more than a dozen new models. If you thought that pace was crazy, don’t expect things to slow down anytime soon.

Anthropic is preparing to release a new model that is better in its reasoning and intuition than the Anthropic models that are currently available commercially, according to a person who has used it. The unreleased model is especially good at discerning a person’s underlying intentions and goals even if they don’t give the model much information, such as explicitly stating those goals, the person said. 

For instance, a person might ask the model to fix a single bug, and the model might go off and instead identify the underlying class of problems that caused the bug and ask whether it should fix the whole class of problems, said the person who has used it.

The Anthropic model is also better at thinking outside of the box rather than regurgitating common sense advice or solutions, the person said. For instance, if a user asks for advice on how to invest in stocks, rather than providing generic advice like looking at price-to-earnings ratios, the model might come up with its own creative algorithms to predict future stock performance, the person said.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Apple sure takes its own sweet time. On Monday, the company sent out invitations to a product announcement happening next Wednesday, which the company’s marketing chief teased in a message on X: “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week.” That’s likely a reference to a new MacBook Pro from the company, which Bloomberg has reported will be Apple’s first touchscreen laptop.

Apparently pigs really do fly. For over a decade, Apple has treated touchscreen laptops like some kind of mutant offspring of computers and tablets, a category it had zero interest in. On a 2012 earnings call, Apple’s then-CEO Tim Cook had a memorable response to a question about the growing number of touchscreen Windows laptops coming on the market: “You can converge a toaster and a refrigerator, but those things are probably not going to be pleasing to the user.” 

“We’re not going to that party,” Cook added. 

A number of things have changed since then. Touchscreens have become somewhat normalized as laptop features. About one in every five notebook computers sold has such capabilities, by one estimate. More recently, Cook handed off the Apple CEO baton to John Ternus, a longtime hardware engineering executive who is much more of a product guy than his predecessor. 

Clearly, a new touchscreen laptop had to have been in the works long before Apple’s leadership transition. Still, it wouldn’t be a surprise to learn that Ternus’ rising stature within the company had something to do with it. Whoever was behind the decision, the first wave of products from the Ternus administration—the iPhone Duo foldable smartphone, HomeView smart display and now possibly a touchscreen MacBook—seems to be sending the message that Apple is ready to embrace categories it previously ignored. That’s a good thing.

Two of the hardest problems in AI right now are creating models that understand the physical world—so called world models—and making sense of the internal workings of AI models—otherwise known as mechanistic interpretability.

Typically, these are treated as two separate problems: researchers working on world models are often not concerned with their internal workings, and interpretability researchers tend to focus on the language models that power most AI tools we currently use. But Sonia Joseph, the co-founder and CEO of a new startup, World Mechanics, argues that world models and interpretability are two sides of the same coin. Joseph joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive to explain that connection, which could be key to making AI useful in the physical world, from medicine to manufacturing. (The full episode is available here.)

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
A hacking group called CyberCartel used a web of AI agents powered by models from companies including Anthropic, SpaceX and Chinese lab Moonshot AI to automate cyberattacks against more than 400 Latin American financial targets, according to an investigation by the cybersecurity startup Straiker.

The research, shared exclusively with The Information, is one of the first detailed reports of cybercriminals using AI models to successfully automate attacks that break into financial institutions. The AI agents used by CyberCartel, which has long targeted Latin American businesses and whose latest targets included banks and payment apps, appear to have stolen passwords and customer data and to have accessed people’s bank accounts autonomously with little human effort, the Straiker research shows.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
In early 2023, Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman gathered with Jas Khaira, the company’s lead AI investor, and other top executives at the finance giant’s Park Avenue headquarters in Manhattan for a debate: Should they give billions of dollars to a little-known data center developer—CoreWeave—that they had turned down just a few months earlier?

CoreWeave had gotten Blackstone to return to the table after landing a multiyear, multibillion-dollar contract to sell cloud computing services to Microsoft. It needed $2.3 billion to buy Nvidia GPUs and secure a data center to house them.

In Blackstone’s discussion of the deal, several executives in the room had deep misgivings, according to a person who attended the meeting. CoreWeave was still something of a mystery, a six-year-old, privately held firm that had generated only $16 million in revenue in the previous year. Schwarzman himself was personally worried his investment team could be making a mistake, the person said.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: Exclusive
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: How CoreWeave’s Debt Binge Brought a Moment of Reckoning

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
OpenAI is bound to get a reality check soon, if it hasn’t already, on how difficult it is to “pace” AI technology, let alone getting all the frontier AI developers to agree on how to do so together.

CEO Sam Altman last week walked employees through three proposals the industry has discussed for how to safely develop AI, we reported yesterday. Those options included plans for developing an international organization akin to the International Atomic Energy Agency; merging the frontier labs into a single entity that would develop, test and distribute models; or a scenario, however far-fetched, in which one lab races ahead of the others and literally crushes their GPUs, ending their ability to catch up.

It goes without saying that each of those options has major issues. But we’ll say it anyway.
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.label: AI Agenda
tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.title: OpenAI’s ‘Pacing 2.0’ Problem: How Smart Is Too Smart?

That’s on top of more than $7 billion it has invested or agreed to invest directly in AI cloud providers.

Nvidia is in talks to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptly pulled its initial public offering early this month, according to people familiar with the talks.

The discussion indicates that Nvidia is likely to continue backing a group of unproven firms known as neoclouds that is facing financial pressure after they stacked up on debt to purchase Nvidia graphics processing units for data centers. Nvidia has already put more than $170 billion on the line for such firms and other large customers, including credit guarantees to help them raise the debt, according to The Information’s analysis.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Ideas are flowing fast and furious on how AI labs can “pace” AI development so safeguards keep up with the technology’s smarts. Last week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman laid out three scenarios he said have been considered in the industry, including merging all of the AI labs into a single entity to develop new AI safely or creating a global regulatory body like the International Atomic Energy Agency.

In the background, a loose group of safety advocates and researchers have been pushing for AI companies to cap the amount of compute they put towards research and development, a limitation they argue would be particularly effective in slowing AI development.

The researchers are proposing companies commit to dedicating at least some minimum share of their computational resources to safety or monitoring, and another minimum share to running AI for customers, otherwise known as inference. That would limit the share of compute that could be used to develop stronger AI capabilities through R&D, such as training new models.

That time has come, according to an example we reported about today. And it looks like hackers don’t even need a Mythos-class model to automate powerful cyberattacks.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Cybersecurity has been a dealmaking bright spot amid the broader software gloom, fueled by bets that AI adoption will boost demand for security products. But it’s been hard for private equity firms to get in on the sizzling sector. 

Corporate buyers have been snapping up cybersecurity companies, competition that makes it harder for private equity firms to buy at prices that leave room for attractive returns when they eventually sell. Rising interest rates further limit what the firms can pay in debt-heavy buyouts. 

That makes Thoma Bravo–backed cybersecurity company Proofpoint’s agreement last week to acquire data security company Varonis Systems in a $6.3 billion deal a notable example of how private equity can still find an opening in a hot market. And the tech-focused private equity giant is likely to do at least one more deal around this size in the coming year. 

The proposed acquisition values Varonis at around six times forward annual recurring revenue, according to a person close to the deal. That’s a discount compared to similar public companies like cloud security and compliance company Qualys, which is trading at around 8 times forward annual recurring revenue. 

Cybersecurity acquisitions were already booming heading into this year, including Alphabet’s $32 billion agreement to buy Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ roughly $25 billion deal for CyberArk, both announced in 2025. But interest in the sector has intensified amid much-hyped releases of powerful models like Anthropic’s Mythos and a series of hacking incidents and agents gone rogue. It could further increase after Wednesday’s disclosure of AI finding a security flaw in open-source programming language PHP, which most websites use.

“People ended up realizing that the…threat vector effectively multiplied to infinity,” said Brian Thom, a managing director at middle market investment bank Brown Gibbons Lang & Co. with a focus on infrastructure software and cybersecurity.

Cybersecurity mergers and acquisitions hit a record 170 transactions in Europe and North America during the third quarter, according to an Arrowpoint Advisory report from earlier this month. Corporate buyers have been particularly active, including Accenture, which this summer acquired a majority stake in industrial cybersecurity company Dragos, plus two smaller companies in deals with a combined enterprise value of more than $4 billion. 

Thoma Bravo, for its part, saw an opportunity as Varonis’ stock price came under pressure. Varonis has spent recent years moving customers from licenses to cloud-based subscriptions, temporarily depressing revenue growth, and announced late last year it would phase out older software by the end of 2026. Its shares had tumbled nearly 50% from last October to around $33 this June, right before reports of a potential takeover surfaced. 

More broadly, some software-focused private equity firms are hunting for companies with depressed share prices but still-credible growth prospects that can hold up even under threat of AI disruption. And many are still nursing the hangover from a software binge during the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. 

The Varonis acquisition comes at a critical time for Thoma Bravo, which has owned Proofpoint since taking it over for $12.3 billion in 2021. Proofpoint is generating more than $1 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, excluding the proposed Varonis acquisition, the person said, while five years under Thoma Bravo ownership puts it at the point when private equity firms typically face growing pressure to cash out. 

Adding Varonis expands Proofpoint’s capabilities beyond its traditional focus of protecting employees from cyberattacks, including phishing and other email threats, to securing sensitive corporate data and controlling who can access it, including employees and AI agents. Though Proofpoint has made previous acquisitions under Thoma Bravo, the Varonis deal is by far its largest and gives it a bigger foothold in AI-related defenses that could arguably help it become a more compelling candidate for an initial public offering. 

Thoma Bravo could be on the hunt for more multibillion-dollar cybersecurity acquisitions following the Varonis deal, which is set to close in the first half of 2027. 

“There’s a finite number of very large cybercompanies that we can invest in,” said Andrew Almeida, a Thoma Bravo partner who oversees cybersecurity and infrastructure software investments. 

The firm is particularly interested in companies that generate revenue from the growing use of AI agents rather than relying solely on traditional pricing models that charge based on the number of human users, he said, and it plans to have another deal similar to the size of Varonis within the next 12 months. 

“Having agentic revenue, not just an agentic vision, but agentic revenue, is a must. And then having a pricing model that can capture this upcoming and ongoing explosion of agents is also a must,” Almeida added. 

Wobbly IPO Window

All eyes are on when Anthropic will finally make its IPO paperwork public, marking one of the final steps toward its hotly anticipated debut. Anthropic announced it had confidentially filed in June, and by late summer was preparing for an IPO as soon as late September.  Now the latest chatter is that the filing could appear by the end of this week. 

Other AI-related IPOs that initially looked poised to go ahead of Anthropic’s have been pulled or delayed amid mounting concerns about the costs of financing data centers and chips, while the broader IPO market has lost momentum in the midst of Treasury volatility. That’s raised questions about who will test the market next—and whether Anthropic’s offering could revive IPOs in general. Some IPO advisers, however, say other companies may need to go public first, paving the way for the AI giant. 

“I don’t think Anthropic going public is going to open the floodgates,” said Edward Best, co-chair of Willkie Farr & Gallagher’s capital markets practice. “I think that Anthropic is going to wait until the water starts moving, and then if Anthropic comes through, it’s just going to widen the river.

“They can’t take the risk that they don’t do well. They’re going to wait until they see a better path, and then other people are going to join right afterwards,” he added.

At first, the X headlines this morning about the latest AI-powered cybersecurity incident seemed dire. But by the time I had a cup of coffee and began parsing all the cyber jargon, I was reassured that an apparent solution was on its way to plug a major new security hole that could make websites vulnerable to cyberintrusions. Since August, a coalition led by OpenAI has been working to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language that undergirds the web. But there was bad news, too: This type of long-simmering response to the latest AI-discovered vulnerabilities may not be viable for much longer. 

For months, OpenAI has been harping on what it calls the “defender’s window”—the critical period of time when cybersecurity experts, armed with advanced AI models, can identify and patch vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them first. The issue is that the gap is rapidly narrowing between cybercapable models from leading U.S. frontier labs and Chinese open-source models, which lack the restrictions U.S. labs impose on their models’ capabilities. Anthropic said as much in a blog post from late September warning that Chinese lab Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 model only lags the U.S. frontier models by about four months. 

The good news: The Trump administration has a shiny new organization created for moments just like these. It’s called the Super Intelligence Force, a name that may elicit eyerolls from some of our more jaded readers. Still, I have heard over and over that all the AI industry wants is coordination and clarity from the White House. That, presumably, is what the SI Force will offer, led by heavy hitters including National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and senior Defense Department official Emil Michael. 

An OpenAI spokesperson told me today that they had briefed several agencies, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, about the PHP vulnerability, as well as briefing Clayton and Michael late last week, representing the first “major engagement” between OpenAI and the SI Force. The spokesperson added that the SI Force provided a central point to coordinate their communication across the broader government. According to a White House official, the SI Force’s work involved helping to put pressure on the “relevant parties” to deploy a vulnerability patch. 

While the SI Force’s coordination function may not seem terribly ambitious, at least it’s a start. It’s worth remembering that the White House essentially had to reorient its entire AI policy in April with the announcement of Mythos. The arrival of Chinese cybercapable open models could represent a Mythos 2.0 moment. I spoke with one former White House official who told me solutions from even a few months ago, like the July Gold Eagle clearinghouse that allows organizations and government agencies to share and fix software vulnerabilities, might already be outdated. It’s up to the SI Force to create a path forward. The next major internet bug likely won’t have the luxury of a two-month-long defender’s window.

Meta’s Performance

On Sunday, in a preview of this week’s Meta Platforms earnings report, your regular Briefing columnist, Martin Peers, declared: “If Meta can stay on investors’ good sides, an equity offering seems in the cards.” Martin nailed it on both accounts. On Wednesday afternoon, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg delivered a bunch of (mostly) good news that had investors in the company purring like kittens. Meta also announced the creation of a new category of common stock that will allow it to raise capital to fund its hefty AI investments without sacrificing Zuckerberg’s control. 

The highlights: For the third quarter, its revenue grew 26% to $64.6 billion, slightly above what the company had forecast. It’s trimming the losses from its Reality Labs unit. While it showed negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion rather than the positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion in the year-earlier period, that was due to its AI investments, and the number wasn’t as bad as some analysts had expected. The company’s anticipated capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion for the full year, while eye-popping, were still within the range it had previously forecast. That was reassuring for investors who’ve gotten spooked in the past by sudden leaps in tech company spending on AI.

Perhaps equally comforting were Zuckerberg’s reassurances that investors will see a payoff from some of its most expensive AI initiatives. He described Muse, Meta’s new agent app, as a bona fide hit for the company, one that has gained 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada in its first six weeks on the market—a faster pace of growth than for its Threads app. While Zuckerberg said the product will remain free for most people, he described a number of ways Meta plans to eventually get paid for it, including commerce transaction fees paid by businesses and money power users will pay for access to advanced models and extra tokens. Meta shares rose 2% in after-hours trading.

Meta also warned of some potentially expensive new legal costs on the horizon, including from lawsuits related to child safety legal cases. During the third quarter, Meta said, its operating income declined 37% from a year earlier to just under $13 billion, due in large part to a nearly $10 billion charge related to legal proceedings. In August, the company settled a child online safety case with 52 attorneys general for $18.59 billion. And on Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

Meta did not say when it plans to raise capital through a new equity offering, or how much it might raise. Presumably, that will happen after Jan. 19, the effective date for issuance of the new nonvoting Class C common stock the company announced today. The company’s existing shareholders will receive a dividend of one Class C share for each share of Class A or B common stock they hold. And crucially, when the company raises money in the future with its Class C stock, that won’t dilute Zuckerberg’s voting power. “The creation of the Class C common stock will continue the founder-led model that has driven the company’s success since its inception,” Meta said.—Nick Wingfield

Tongue-Tied at Tesla

On Tesla’s earnings call, Elon Musk had much less to say on the topic of a potential merger of the EV maker with his other company, SpaceX, than he did Tuesday afternoon on SpaceX’s earnings call. He told investors he had said everything he wanted to on the topic for now. Tesla’s automotive revenues fell 3% to $20.56 billion while its total revenues remained flat at $28 billion compared to a year earlier. Tesla shares fell 3% in after-hours trading.—Nick Wingfield 

In Other News

  • Electronic Arts plans to shed around 400 jobs, or about 3% of its staff, and shut down its BioWare studio, Bloomberg reported. 
  • Microsoft asked shareholders to approve a plan to lower CEO Satya Nadella’s pay by 6% due to falling revenue in its Xbox unit. The company also nominated Stripe co-founder John Collison to its board.
  • Google will stop requiring local government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements when it plans to build data centers in their areas.

When Reflection AI set out to raise $2.5 billion early this year, one of its existing venture backers, B Capital, was eager to invest again in the startup, which has emerged as the most high-profile U.S. maker of open-source AI models. But Reflection’s valuation had more than tripled in just six months, forcing investors to write big checks for a sizable stake.

Such a check would have been too big for B Capital’s main venture fund, a $500 million vehicle raised in July. To come up with the cash, the company turned to a different source of capital: a pool of money apart from its regular fund, designed to give limited partners—the pension funds, endowments and wealthy individuals that back VC firms—more direct access to hot startups like Reflection at reduced fees.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
While much of the AI industry has fixated on new personal AI assistants from Meta and OpenAI, video AI is enjoying a quiet renaissance. Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg is teaming up with the former head of OpenAI’s Sora app to launch a new AI film company. Startup Higgsfield quadrupled its valuation to $5.4 billion in August. And Kling AI, the video unit of Chinese social media giant Kuaishou Technology, raised nearly $3 billion at a $15 billion valuation over the summer.

The latest video AI company to seize this moment is Utopai Studios, a 4-year-old film startup based in Mountain View, Calif. Utopai closed a funding round for $60 million that valued it at $1 billion and has already received term sheets for a subsequent round that would value the company at $2 billion to $3 billion, according to someone close to the company. 

The enthusiasm for video AI startups follows improvements in the quality and length of the clips that video AI models can generate. In September, Higgsfield announced that it had crossed $1 billion in annualized revenue, showing that the technology has serious commercial potential.

SB Energy, the SoftBank Group–controlled developer of a massive planned Ohio data center project for OpenAI, is considering going public in December or possibly waiting until next year, according to people familiar with the discussions.

That is a later timeline than previously expected. The data center developer was aiming to go public as soon as September, The Information reported in August. But since then, the public market has soured on initial public offerings from data center and AI cloud companies. Australian cloud firm Firmus yanked its IPO plans earlier this month, and others are considering delaying their offerings.

Enterprise software firm Datadog recently offered to buy Israeli cloud cybersecurity startup Upwind Security for nearly $4 billion, according to someone with direct knowledge of the talks, the latest sign of white-hot interest in such firms.

Upwind has fielded other takeover attempts from multiple bidders in recent months but hasn’t accepted any offers. It is finalizing a $300 million funding round at a roughly $3.8 billion valuation, meaning the Datadog offer doesn’t carry much of a premium over the private valuation, said two people with knowledge of the situation. The startup sells software to keep tabs on applications, including so-called AI agents, that run in the cloud and to detect and automatically respond to potential evidence of hacks or breaches.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
Salesforce is leading the software industry’s attempt to collect fees from businesses that use Claude and other external AI tools to automate work in enterprise apps.

As soon as next month, Salesforce plans to require companies to register outside AI agents, a step toward charging them each time those agents update or analyze data stored in Salesforce. The fees let Salesforce earn money from customers who use such AI instead of paying for Salesforce’s built-in AI products. 

The Salesforce tollgate has implications for the rest of the industry, which is coming to terms with the idea that so-called AI agents may be able to use software firms’ apps more efficiently than humans do, meaning their seat-based or per-user pricing model might not have staying power. The question is whether the new AI tollgates—which Atlassian, Workday, ServiceNow and Datadog are also erecting to various extents—and other pricing shifts will more than make up for an eventual decline in per-seat subscription revenues. 

The vast majority of workers haven’t yet outsourced such work to AI, of course, and companies like Salesforce are trying to get more revenue from them as well. They charge fees based on how much they use the apps’ built-in AI tools and are also experimenting with outcome-based pricing, meaning customers only pay when such tools actually complete a task successfully or help the customers make more money.

For now, Salesforce and some other software firms developing tollgates for customers’ AI agents haven’t started charging the tolls. They’re letting customers experiment for free with the technology a little while longer. (The customers still have to pay providers such as Anthropic to use the AI agents in the first place.)

Starting around November, according to the company’s website, Salesforce will require customers to register any externally-made AI agents if they plan to use them to take actions on their behalf in Salesforce apps. Each action an agent takes in Salesforce counts as a billable “interaction,” according to the company. The move has lifted investor confidence in Salesforce recently.

Salesforce describes the registration requirement as a security measure because the company gives each agent its own identity and narrower data-access permissions, compared to humans. It isn’t clear how Salesforce will clamp down on customers using their own AI agents, such as OpenClaw-powered ones that run on a person’s computer and can access any app that runs on it. (Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.)

Salesforce hasn’t announced prices tied to such agent usage, but customers could eventually end up paying a lot more money than they do now, given how many of them are already using their own AI on top of Salesforce apps and bypassing Salesforce’s own built-in AI tools, according to software consultants and chief information officers. 

Nick Hamm, a software consultant, said that most of the 150 enterprises he works with are currently using AI from Anthropic and OpenAI to automate work inside Salesforce apps, for free. But they’re reconsidering that usage in anticipation of the upcoming fees. If the fees are too high, the customers may move their business data outside of Salesforce’s apps so they can use AI to analyze the data without paying an extra cost, he said.

New customers will have a three month grace period after the new pricing is announced to register their AI agents, and the pricing won’t affect existing customers until their contracts are renewed. 

In addition to the billable “interactions,” customers have the option to buy unlimited agent usage by purchasing a “headless license,” a Salesforce account executive told Hamm in a LinkedIn message viewed by The Information. 

Some customers such as Lumen, a fiber-optic network provider to enterprises and data centers, say they are waiting to test Salesforce’s new connectors until pricing is disclosed.

So far, Lumen has leaned on Salesforce’s built-in AI. A longtime customer of Salesforce’s customer relationship management software, Lumen made a “major” investment in using Salesforce’s AI sales agents in the last 12 months, according to CIO Jim Fowler. The sales agents help with tasks such as collecting customer information and generating sales quotes for the customers to buy fiber connections between data centers, saving Lumen’s human salespeople considerable time, he said.

So far, Fowler said, Salesforce has been “super flexible” about letting Lumen use existing subscription fees to also cover its use of built-in AI features such as the sales agents.

Early customer reactions to the pricing announcement will likely determine how flexible Salesforce is with customers that start renewing their contracts after November. If its past AI pricing efforts are any guide, Salesforce could easily switch things up depending on the feedback, or any blowback, it receives.
