Greetings!  

On their earnings calls earlier in the week, Meta Platforms and SpaceX delivered the same underlying message to investors: demand for AI is running ahead of the supply of AI compute. On Thursday, another important player in the AI ecosystem—Blackstone, the alternative asset management giant—repeated a version of that refrain. 

On its own earnings call, the firm, a major investor at the center of the AI data center boom, faced pointed questions from analysts about rising financing costs and mounting investor concerns over the sustainability of the buildout. Its executives argued that the very factors threatening the AI industry’s expansion could actually work in Blackstone’s favor. CEO Steve Schwarzman noted that constraints on power availability and growing public opposition to new data centers are making it harder to bring new capacity online, potentially making existing facilities more valuable. Blackstone President Jon Gray also suggested the firm could seek higher returns on projects where it hasn’t signed leases yet in order to offset rising borrowing costs. 

Blackstone’s third-quarter results offered some support for that argument: Its infrastructure investments were buoyed by what executives called “extraordinary” data center leasing momentum, significantly outperforming its broader private equity and real estate holdings. “Despite all the negative things you’re reading about AI today, when we look across our business, this continues to be the area where we’re driving the highest returns,” Gray said during the call. 

But it’s hard to ignore the fact that the financing concerns and roadblocks threatening the broader AI infrastructure buildout are also hitting closer to home for Blackstone. Fears about rising financing costs have sent CoreWeave’s stock and bond prices plunging—the neocloud’s shares closed down another 10% Thursday after sliding last week—while Australian AI cloud provider Firmus abruptly pulled its initial public offering earlier this month. Blackstone has provided billions in loans to CoreWeave and has both invested in and lent money to Firmus. 

Blackstone has also been pressing ahead with brand-new AI ventures. In May, the firm announced an initial $5 billion equity commitment to a joint venture with Google to create a new cloud company that will use Google’s TPU chips, with plans to bring 500 megawatts of capacity online by next year. The venture could need as much as $25 billion in total investment, including some borrowed money, and it has reportedly encountered delays at potential data center sites. 

Blackstone, for its part, says that broader anxiety about AI hasn’t undermined its ability to raise fresh cash for making its own investments. “We’re continuing to be able to raise capital. Obviously investors are asking the same question around AI, but what we continue to see is demand and usage of the AI going up faster than the compute,” Gray said.

While Blackstone says it wants to continue going big in AI, it can only finance a tiny portion of the industry’s broader infrastructure buildout itself. The trillions of dollars of financing needed for chips and data centers in the coming years requires raising money from a far broader pool of investors. Blackstone itself has said it’s not clear where all the money will come from. 

Jas Khaira, the head of the team leading Blackstone’s push into AI investment, said late last month that the firm is still trying to determine which investors across the public debt and private credit markets will be able to provide the funding needed to sustain the buildout. 

“We have not mapped out who’s going to buy all the debt. We have some hypotheses, but the honest answer is we don’t know where all of it will come from,” he said at The Information’s AI Agenda event in San Francisco.

Data Center Headwinds

Despite Blackstone’s overall positive note on AI demand, we got fresh evidence Thursday afternoon of the uncertainty in the IPO market for companies in the data center business. Phoebe Liu and Valida Pau had a scoop that SB Energy, a company controlled by SoftBank Group that is developing an OpenAI data center in Ohio, is discussing a plan to put off its IPO until December or earlier next year. Previously, SB Energy was aiming to go public in September. The best hope for an SB Energy IPO is that the supply of AI compute gets so tight that investors start warming back up to data centers.—Nick Wingfield   

In Other News

In April 2025, Eric Glyman, co-founder and co-CEO of Ramp, received some bad news: A deal was falling apart.

Glyman had been hoping Ramp, a highly valued startup that sells corporate credit cards and expense management software, could strike a partnership with Airwallex—a fast-growing fintech founded in Melbourne, Australia—that would improve Ramp’s ability to handle international payments. But now Airwallex CEO Jack Zhang was pulling the plug on the proposed deal—partly because of pressure from investors who wanted his company to compete with Ramp, according to employees of both companies.

Glyman made an attempt to salvage the partnership, according to people familiar with discussions between the two companies. Zhang demurred. Soon after, Glyman warned Zhang that the relationship between their companies might not be so friendly in the future, according to people familiar with the situation.

In the wake of the canceled deal, some of Ramp’s high-profile, politically connected investors have launched a public and private campaign to urge the U.S. government to saddle Airwallex with a government investigation that probes any links the company may have with the Chinese government. Those investors have alleged that the Chinese government could access customer data passing through Airwallex subsidiaries in China.

Welcome, Weekenders!

Whenever I’m the slightest bit ill, I take to my bed and mope. If it goes more than a day or so, I assume the worst—that the end is nigh. I can’t honestly remember the last time I felt unwell for more than a couple days, but I imagine such a scenario would probably find me consulting ChatGPT about burial shrouds.

So I’d like to extend a smidgen of sympathy to CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator. Surely, he’s been feeling poorly for nearly two weeks!

In the last 12 days, CoreWeave’s stock has been nearly halved. A confluence of factors has contributed to the rampant decline, as my colleague Dakin Campbell explained. In short, investors are worried about how rising interest rates will affect CoreWeave’s ability to raise debt, which it needs to fund its business of selling cloud computing services. They’re also concerned about whether CoreWeave can handle the costs of the mound of debt it already has.

Last week, fresh data on U.S. inflation fueled interest rate concerns: Inflation jumped in September, increasing the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates—making all debt more expensive. 

Even though there was no new inflation data this week, CoreWeave shares continued to fall—from around $60 on Monday to roughly $54 on Friday. Not even Nvidia’s all-powerful CEO, Jensen Huang, was able to stanch the bleeding when he tried to sound a note of confidence for CoreWeave on Thursday, saying the demand for companies like CoreWeave—neoclouds—is “off the charts.”

The stock nerds over at Barron’s tried to argue that Wednesday’s earnings report from SpaceX is actually a good sign for CoreWeave. Those numbers showed surging demand for SpaceX’s nascent business of selling its excess AI compute, but I’m not sure whether that necessarily bodes well for the company. Yes, an indicator of demand for compute could be interpreted as a welcome data point for CoreWeave, a compute seller. But SpaceX’s compute business increasingly seems like a real competitor to CoreWeave and other neoclouds, and as the much, much better established company, SpaceX has the resources to fund expansion of its compute-selling efforts without acquiring hazardous amounts of debt. And investors are a great deal less likely to sink its stock price over interest rate jitters.

More news from Wednesday highlighted the industry’s appetite for compute. Meta Platforms said it will create a new share class in January—essentially a two-for-one stock split—that will allow it to reach for more capital to spend on AI. It’s also partly a maneuver that would help CEO Mark Zuckerberg pay off California’s billionaire tax if the levy is approved next month. Meta’s board justified helping Zuck pay his taxes by saying that the CEO had threatened to pick up sticks and leave California—and that it was essential to have him in the office as much as possible. (I had to laugh. Just a couple years ago, Zuckerberg was telling us the metaverse would arrive soon, and we’d all be living as digital stick things. Such was the potential of the metaverse that Zuckerberg renamed his entire company for it. Well, guess not!) 

More capital at Meta might be good for CoreWeave. Meta is a CoreWeave customer—to the tune of $35 billion. There’s no guarantee, of course, that Meta will take a newfound gusher of capital and go back to CoreWeave again. Recently, Meta has been building its own data centers and readying production of its custom AI chips. It has also considered selling compute.

Investors looked on wearily at Meta’s stock split/potential Zuck gift, with the company’s shares dropping nearly 9% on Thursday. In fact, Meta’s moves unnerved the entire market yet again over how much this whole AI thing will cost. The Nasdaq sank 2.6% on Thursday. CoreWeave shares fell 10%, while declines also hit Nebius (down 7.2%) and IREN (8.3%), the two other publicly traded neoclouds. And everything kept falling on Friday. 

Are all the stock moves based on buttoned-up rationality? No. But like the common cold that I’m always certain will put me six feet under, worry on Wall Street is contagious.—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Bear Brook: A Private Matter”

Back in 2017, NHPR, a little public radio station in New Hampshire, found itself with a hit national podcast, “Bear Brook,” about cold-case murders—four bodies in two barrels stashed in Bear Brook State Park—and the genetic testing involved in investigating the crimes. Reporter Jason Moon followed up with a second season about a different crime in 2023 and now returns with a third season about another weird happening: the disappearance of 76-year-old Jay Hickey, a local Christmas tree farmer. (Moon likens the setting to a Hallmark movie—frankly, it gave me distinct “Twin Peaks” vibes.) After Hickey vanished one autumn, it was months before anyone went looking for him. That was strange because he was suffering from dementia, so surely his wife, Pat, would’ve, uh, noticed he wasn’t around, right? Obviously she offed him, right? Perhaps, but she clearly was suffering from something herself. It’s the type of tale that could be glossed over with schlock, sordid storytelling. That’s definitely not Moon’s approach.—Abram Brown

Reading: “Kobuk the Destroyer” by Alex Davies

Just in the past 12 hours, I’ve dodged a number of possible catastrophes: I was not singed by my hair dryer, crushed by my office’s elevator doors or left unproductive by a bunch of buttons tumbling out of my keyboard. I owe my good fortune to the rigorous science of product testing, a gorpy-seeming topic made into enlightening, witty entertainment in “Kobuk the Destroyer” by Alex Davies, a former Wired magazine editor. It is an ode to the nerd geniuses who devise those tests, but it can also feel like a drop directly onto the factory floor of Looney Tunes’ Acme Corporation,  presenting a sharp critique of how often executives cut corners and ignore blatant problems as they pursue commercialization. Without the centurylong expansion of product testing, we’d all be left in the same position as Wile E. Coyote, with faulty, rocket-powered roller skates attached to our feet.

The titular Kobuk, a grizzly bear, may be one of the most prolific practitioners of the field—having lived out the last several decades at a Montana wildlife sanctuary that partners with a government agency to certify various products as bear proof. Kobuk has the great joy of tearing apart coolers, trash cans, composters, and many other items, and gets rewarded with fish, peanut butter, honey, and dog biscuits for his efforts: Whatever survives Kobuk’s assault receives the certification. Through his efforts, the general public can buy coolers that actually do keep out other Kobuks. Theoretically, that prevents his shaggy-haired brethren from learning to filch food or hang around humans, habits that can get a bear relocated or euthanized. Kobuk has pawed his way onto a noble path initially blazed in the 1920s by Underwriters Laboratories, a Chicago-based business that pioneered the art of product testing—with engineers who assessed the durability of safes by subjecting them to thousand-degree heat, 30-foot drops and kerosene-fueled explosions. Davies keeps up a brisk pace as he winds through the many testing approaches adopted by various industries in the following years, including the NASA wind tunnel used to develop the Curiosity Mars lander and the oval-shaped gelatin sacks that engineers fired into airplane engines to avoid needing to kill thousands and thousands of live birds.

As many of you might surely agree, determining the safety of one group of products in particular remains decidedly challenging: ahem, AI! Much of the alignment training and red teaming that goes into AI development comes away with vague conclusions, Davies writes: We simply don’t understand enough about what we’ve created, and AI often operates much more unpredictably than, say, a refrigerator door or an airbag. Trying to understand why an AI behaved safely in one setting but dangerously in another is “like trying to understand why your dog growls at people carrying shopping bags but not people carrying suitcases.”—A.B.

Watching: “Carrie”

Stephen King’s cabinet of terrors is a well-stocked place, cluttered with weird evils, many with complex, lengthy backstories. The It of “It,” you may recall, is not actually an evil clown—it’s an ageless, alien ball of light. “The Langoliers” is a time-travel story…about piranha-like, interdimensional critters that literally eat time. I could try to also get into the motivations of Randall Flagg in “The Stand,” but unlike King, I don’t have 823 pages to do that here. 

The knottier of King’s novels defy easy screen adaptations. Other retellings of King stories fail on the screen largely because they suffer in comparison to finer, earlier movie adaptations, to say nothing of their misappropriation of King’s material. 

On Amazon, there’s an excellent new restructuring of King’s “Carrie,” his first bestseller and, of course, the source for a much-loved film by director Brian De Palma, which put both De Palma and King on the map. There’s a simplicity and universal resonance to King’s story of tortured, telekinetic high schooler Carrie White that makes it highly moldable: Teenagers have been terrifying ever since there have been teenagers, both to themselves and to those around them.

Amazon’s “Carrie” was helmed by Mike Flanagan, who has a string of spooky series on Netflix (“The Fall of the House of Usher,” “The Haunting of Hill House”) and did the 2019 movie adaptation of King’s “Doctor Sleep.” Flanagan adeptly positions his “Carrie” in the modern day. The infamous shower scene, for example, does not really end when Carrie (newcomer Summer Howell) is escorted away by kindhearted PE teacher Miss Desjardin (Amber Midthunder). Her bullying classmates captured the entire thing on their cellphones, and their torment of her continues via an anonymous Instagram account. Later, her mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan), a religious nut who also favors QAnon-like conspiracy theories, seizes the internet as a means for her own ferocious manipulations. 

With the benefit of an eight-episode run, Flanagan gets the opportunity to give greater depth to the Whites and the people around them, including Carrie’s chief bully, Christine (Alison Thornton), and classmate Sue (Siena Agudong), who befriends Carrie in this version. Granted, it might seem like Flanagan is trying to stretch the material as thin as a funeral crepe. He doesn’t, aided by roundly top-notch performances.—A.B.

tag:www.theinformation.com,2005:Article/.content:
The tech industry equivalent of the Super Bowl may finally be upon us. Anthropic could make public the paperwork for its initial public offering as early as Monday. Details about Anthropic’s finances from either drafts of the IPO filing or recent investor meetings have been dribbling out for weeks. As a result, some of the S-1’s revelations will not be, well, all that revelatory. 

But there are still many, many mysteries about Anthropic the filing could clear up, or at least make a little less fuzzy. I asked my colleagues Jason Dean and Laura Mandaro for their shortlist of items they hope the S-1 will illuminate:      

• More financial details. More clarity on Anthropic’s trajectory toward profitability, along with cash flow numbers and other operational financial metrics that haven’t yet leaked out. 

• Ownership, investment and revenue details from big partners. Hopefully, the filing will confirm just how much money Anthropic is paying Google and Amazon to run its AI on their servers, along with details about how much those companies invested in Anthropic and how much those stakes have appreciated. 

• Who pays Anthropic’s bills. Anthropic has said around a fifth of its revenue this quarter of its revenue in the first half of this year came from just two customers, compared to a quarter for all of 2025, according to published reports. Investors will look for more recent concentration data and additional details on the sources of its revenue. Historically, most of its revenue has come from sales of its AI via an application programming interface, but these can rise and fall depending on what model is hot among developers. We’re looking for details on revenue from its Claude subscriptions as well as through other companies like Amazon that resell Anthropic AI in exchange for a cut of those sales.

• More on governance. Many idiosyncrasies of Anthropic’s mission-minded corporate structure are public. For instance, a group of non-shareholders called the Long-Term Benefit Trust appoints the majority of its board. As we’ve reported, in the run-up to the IPO, Anthropic developed a plan to grant its seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, a combined 50.1% of voting power even if they reduce some of their stakes. What we don’t know is whether Amodei has any particular power over the six other founders and how exactly Anthropic will resolve conflicts between the trust and board members appointed by the founders. (Anthropic has planned to give employees a special class of stock for tiebreaker votes—complicated!)

• Lockups and secondary sales. We’ve written that Anthropic has mulled extending the lockups—the period when most shareholders are barred from selling their stock—beyond the typical 180-day period. But the company has considered making an exception for some shareholders at the time of the IPO, allowing what’s known as a secondary sale at the listing. Such sales would contrast with other tech IPOs this year that didn’t allow secondary sales during their listings, such as SpaceX and Cerebras. We’re looking for how long most investors have to sit on their shares and which groups of investors—or employees—can bail more quickly. 

More Ahead

The Anthropic filing fireworks aren’t the only big events in tech we’ll be watching next week. There’s also:

• Earnings reports from the three major hyperscalers. Google and Microsoft are scheduled to report on Wednesday, while Amazon will report on Thursday. Any changes the companies announce to their data center spending plans or forecasts about AI demand are likely to move the already jittery markets. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy isn’t waiting until earnings to strike a bullish note on the performance of AWS, his cloud unit. In an Andreessen Horowitz podcast published Friday, Jassy said AWS is “largely sold out” of computing capacity through the end of next year. He also said the company’s decade-old acquisition of Annapurna Labs, a semiconductor startup behind AWS’ custom AI chip and other processors, may end up being Amazon’s best deal ever.

• Instacart’s next move. On Friday, we broke the news that Instacart is exploring a possible sale of the company and has held preliminary conversations with DoorDash and Uber. Our story said that talks with Uber appear to have fizzled. But it will be interesting to see if a deal with someone else comes together. Instacart and DoorDash are due to report earnings on Nov. 5 and 4, respectively. Expect analysts to grill the companies about the prospects for a deal, if one isn’t announced by then.

• New Apple devices. Apple is having an event on Wednesday where it’s expected to announce its first touchscreen MacBook, as we mentioned earlier in the week. Get ready for some greasy MacBook screens.

In Other News

  • AI has delivered no financial payoff to U.S. companies other than tech companies, Torsten Slock, chief economist at private equity firm Apollo Global Management argued in an essay. 
  • China’s Moonshot AI on Friday announced a new model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, that rivals the performance of leading U.S. frontier models on some benchmarks. 
  • Instacart shares closed up 9% on Friday after The Information reported that the grocery delivery company is exploring options to sell itself.

Before we get to today’s column, the big day is here: Anthropic dropped its long-awaited public S-1 filing Monday morning. Tune in today for stories from my colleagues and me that will be breaking down the most important takeaways from the filing, such as improvements in the company’s compute efficiency, details on its spending and cash burn, and interesting new disclosures that could point to an eventual end to its unusual Long-Term Benefit Trust, a group of non-shareholders who advise the company on safety and social issues and can appoint a majority of its board.

Onto today’s column...

It seems like every AI startup financing these days has multiple tranches in which different investors get in at different valuations. At first, it was unusual to see just two tranches. Now we see extra-hot funding rounds with three tranches or more.

It’s no secret that investors aren’t thrilled about these multi-tranche rounds (specifically, the investors that can’t get in at the lower valuation). Some of them argue that the practice allows bigger venture capital firms to flex their power and force smaller VC firms into the second, more expensive tranche. They also say it allows the startup to claim a bigger valuation, even though some or most of the new capital came in at a lower price. 

But founders and many investors tell me that the unique capital needs of AI companies, which are eternally starved of enough servers, is driving these unusual structures.
